- The shape $R$ is a rhombus. Therefore, it has two pairs of congruent sides that are adjacent to each other, so it is a kite.

- The shape $S$ is a parallelogram. Any two adjacent sides are not congruent with each other, therefore, it is not a kite.

random variable $X∼\text{Po}(11)$ given below, compute $P(X<10).$

| $\,x\,$ | $7$ | $8$ | $9$ | $10$ | $11$ | $12$ | $13$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X\le x)$ | $\,0.1432\,$ | $\,0.2320\,$ | $\,0.3405\,$ | $\,0.4599\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.6887\,$ | $\,0.7813\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<10) & =P(X\in \{0,1,…,9\}) \\  & =P(X\le 9) \\  & =F(9) \\  & =0.3405.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163956 :answer-field/correct 17592186163961 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166737 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d8455b7b-7c5b-5bab-ac5b-3afa70d37c46"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167152 :question/problem "Using the cumulative distribution function table of the Poisson random variable $X∼\text{Po}(6)$ given below, compute $P(2<X\le 5).$

| $\,x\,$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X\le x)$ | $\,0.0620\,$ | $\,0.1512\,$ | $\,0.2851\,$ | $\,0.4457\,$ | $\,0.6063\,$ | $\,0.7440\,$ | $\,0.8472\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x).
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(5) & =P(X\le 5) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,…,5\}) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,2\})+P(X\in \{3,4,5\}) \\  & =P(X\le 2)+P(2<X\le 5) \\  & =F(2)+P(2<X\le 5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<X\le 5) & =F(5)-F(2) \\  & =0.4457-0.0620 \\  & =0.3837.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163962 :answer-field/correct 17592186163967 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-d8455b7b-7c5b-5bab-ac5b-3afa70d37c46" :question/id #uuid "d8455b7b-7c5b-5bab-ac5b-3afa70d37c46" :question/math-academy-id "q-224966" :question/problem "Using the cumulative distribution function table of the Poisson random variable $X∼\text{Po}(8)$ given below, compute $P(4<X\le 6).$

:question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(y-x)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177909 :answer-field/correct "answer-1d03d1d4-83e8-5434-ba88-654e772f6034" :answer-field/choices ["answer-94ef6336-a885-5e0f-9339-fb9e597d51dc" "answer-2bedcbb9-3a20-535c-92e0-bda037bb0531" "answer-1d03d1d4-83e8-5434-ba88-654e772f6034" "answer-c61c8d76-f473-524c-b92c-3be06cc40c20"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94ef6336-a885-5e0f-9339-fb9e597d51dc" :answer/id #uuid "94ef6336-a885-5e0f-9339-fb9e597d51dc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-18\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2bedcbb9-3a20-535c-92e0-bda037bb0531" :answer/id #uuid "2bedcbb9-3a20-535c-92e0-bda037bb0531" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-9\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1d03d1d4-83e8-5434-ba88-654e772f6034" :answer/id #uuid "1d03d1d4-83e8-5434-ba88-654e772f6034" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "18\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c61c8d76-f473-524c-b92c-3be06cc40c20" :answer/id #uuid "c61c8d76-f473-524c-b92c-3be06cc40c20" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204011 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fe1475b2-e88a-5639-9c34-aefc361e0ff5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204445 :question/problem "Consider two sets of $25$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{25},$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{25}.$ You are given that

$$

$$

$$

17592186078250 :question/problem "Find the value of $\cos L.$

![](images/78/78416d3c8ec8a8351ecfe0a4ea81feb05cce29f55dd9ec4bc676e6363dd49ec0.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\cos L = \dfrac {\textrm{adjacent}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {JL}{KL} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $KL.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\eqalign{
KL &= \sqrt{ JK^2 + JL^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ (3)^2 + (3\sqrt3)^2 } \
&= \sqrt{  9 + 27 } \
&= \sqrt{36}\
&= 6\
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
	\cos L &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL} \[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{3\sqrt 3}{6} \[5pt] 
&=\dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2.
}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078393 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aec65431-c1ff-5f84-a471-b95024c34089"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078252 :question/problem "Find the sine of $\angle Y.$

$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-{1.8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9-3.24} \\  & =\sqrt{5.76} \\  & =2.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡O & =\frac{OM}{3} \\  & =\frac{2.4}{3} \\  & =\frac{24}{30} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9e20ba3b-2ce4-5c79-9503-04b8fbe7a3c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9e20ba3b-2ce4-5c79-9503-04b8fbe7a3c4" :answer-field/id #uuid "9e20ba3b-2ce4-5c79-9503-04b8fbe7a3c4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d13eb98c-1c94-5c76-9b4d-87ec446e756d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ad6f986b-c2cd-55e4-a5d3-6fbb550bf5f2" "answer-41461aa7-43de-55b4-80f5-ac43667106ca" "answer-fb73bb44-7d7d-557b-b4d7-55b44301f620" "answer-76bffbe9-0710-5f13-8f49-ff8692ccf9d0" "answer-d13eb98c-1c94-5c76-9b4d-87ec446e756d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ad6f986b-c2cd-55e4-a5d3-6fbb550bf5f2" :answer/id #uuid "ad6f986b-c2cd-55e4-a5d3-6fbb550bf5f2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-41461aa7-43de-55b4-80f5-ac43667106ca" :answer/id #uuid "41461aa7-43de-55b4-80f5-ac43667106ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fb73bb44-7d7d-557b-b4d7-55b44301f620" :answer/id #uuid "fb73bb44-7d7d-557b-b4d7-55b44301f620" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76bffbe9-0710-5f13-8f49-ff8692ccf9d0" :answer/id #uuid "76bffbe9-0710-5f13-8f49-ff8692ccf9d0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d13eb98c-1c94-5c76-9b4d-87ec446e756d" :answer/id #uuid "d13eb98c-1c94-5c76-9b4d-87ec446e756d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078740 :question/problem "![](images/f9/f9f59d4328ad43e6e342da3cf9e87ccd5dfe33b97c46424e7fcc2b9f562fc452.png)

Find the tangent of $∠N.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡N=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{OM}{MN}=\frac{OM}{2.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6.5}^{2}-{2.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{42.25-6.25} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡N & =\frac{OM}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{6}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{60}{25} \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186075316 :answer-field/correct 17592186075317 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079637 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have a right triangle $\triangle ABC$ with legs $AC= BC = 1,$ like the one in the diagram below.
How can we find the value $\sin \theta$ if we don't know one of the relevant sides?

![](images/ae/ae5157e6824fd98861194302ab912e76d9e79dade6706dfbedea97d859f18a79.png)

Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\sin \theta = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {AC}{AB} = \dfrac 1 c
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $c.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{A{C}^{2}+B{C}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can finish computing the value of $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

No matter which trigonometric function we need to find, if we are missing one of the relevant sides but we know the lengths of the other two sides, we can always use the Pythagorean Theorem." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078657 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186373993 :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin.

:question/problem "The weights of the wooden and steel chairs produced by a furniture company have standard deviations of $2\,\text{lb}$ and $1\,\text{lb},$ respectively. The company wants to determine whether the population mean ${\mu }_{x}$ of weights for the wooden chairs is greater than the population mean ${\mu }_{y}$ of weights for the steel chairs. They construct a $95%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means.

Given that the company sampled $100$ wooden chairs and $150$ steel chairs and found that their mean weights are $10\,\text{lb}$ and $9\,\text{lb},$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. The end-points of the $95%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means are approximately $1\pm 0.423.$

II. All values contained within the $95%$ confidence interval are positive.

III. The confidence interval data suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "Notice that 

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=10-9=1
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.025}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.025})=0.025,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.025}=1.960:$ 

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.960\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{2}^{2}}{100}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{150}}≈0.423
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 1\pm 0.423\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. The end-points of our confidence interval are $1\pm 0.423.$

- Statement II is true. All values within the confidence interval are positive:

$$
(1-0.423,\,1+0.423)=(0.577,\,1.423)
$$

- Statement III is true. Since all values within the confidence interval are positive, this suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5298ca4d-ecde-5661-bd4e-59d6462c363f"] :db/ensure from a population with standard deviation ${\sigma }_{1}=3.4$ and a sample of size ${n}_{2}=86$ from a population with standard deviation ${\sigma }_{2}=4.9.$ Given that the samples are independent and the sample means are ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}=34$ and  ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=43,$ find a $95%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.96)=0.025,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$*" :question/worked-solution "Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both sample sizes are "sufficiently large," i.e., $\ge 30,$ and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=34-43=-9
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.96)=0.025.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.025}=1.96.
$$

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.96\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{3.4}^{2}}{58}+\frac{{4.9}^{2}}{86}}≈1.356
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the $95%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means:

$$
\begin{aligned} & -9\pm 1.356\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-21552841-7d86-5c0f-9131-48f4014f0900"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-34a9b0ce-4c8f-5634-aaa8-208faeda7581" :question/id #uuid "34a9b0ce-4c8f-5634-aaa8-208faeda7581" :question/math-academy-id "q-159641" :question/problem "It is known that the thickness of ceramic tiles from suppliers X and Y are normally distributed with standard deviations of ${\sigma }_{x}=1.6\,\text{mm}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}=1.2\,\text{mm},$ respectively. A construction contractor wants to determine whether the population mean ${\mu }_{x}$ of the thickness of ceramic tiles from supplier X is greater than the population mean ${\mu }_{y}$ of the thickness of ceramic tiles from supplier Y. He constructs a $95%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means.

Given that the contractor sampled $20$ tiles from supplier X and $18$ tiles from supplier Y and found that their mean thicknesses are $18.8\,\text{mm}$ and $18.5\,\text{mm},$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. The end-points of the $95%$ confidence interval for the difference between the population means are approximately $0.3\pm 0.894.$

II. All values contained within the $95%$ confidence interval are positive.

III. The confidence interval data suggests that ${\mu }_{x}>{\mu }_{y}.$

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "Notice that

- the samples are independent,

- both populations are normally distributed, and

- both population variances are known.

As a result, given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the difference ${\mu }_{1}-{\mu }_{2}$ between the corresponding population means can be written as

$$
({\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2})\pm E
$$

where 

- $E={z}_{\alpha /2}\sqrt{\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{n}_{1}}+\frac{{\sigma }_{2}^{2}}{{n}_{2}}}$ is the margin of error,

- ${\overset{―}{x}}_{1}$ and ${\overset{―}{x}}_{2}$ are the sample means, ${\mu }_{1}$ and ${\mu }_{2}$ are the population means, ${\sigma }_{1}^{2}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}^{2}$ are the population variances,  ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are the sample sizes,

- $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

Now, to construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1.** Find the point estimate:

$$
{\overset{―}{x}}_{1}-{\overset{―}{x}}_{2}=18.8-18.5=0.3
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a $95%$ confidence interval, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.95=0.05\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.025.
$$

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.025}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.025})=0.025,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$
From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.025}=1.960:$ 

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Now, we can compute the margin of error:

$$
E=1.960\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{1.6}^{2}}{20}+\frac{{1.2}^{2}}{18}}≈0.894
$$

- **Step 3.** Construct the confidence interval:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.3\pm 0.894\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. The end-points of our confidence interval are $0.3\pm 0.894.$

- Statement II is false. The confidence interval contains $0:$

$$
(0.3-0.894,\,0.3+0.894)=(-0.594,\,1.194)
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the confidence interval contains zero, it remains possible that ${\mu }_{x}={\mu }_{y}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f24e3ec2-08cb-5869-8ee2-41217f338f4b"] :db/ensure How can we plot the graph of $y=f(-x)?$

![](images/51/517dbe715d1f1e79756e6e7bd0d733cc5894f425ac02b2ac1bde2c2a33e86c8d.png)

We can use some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ to find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(-x).$

For example, let's take the point $(3,4)$. The fact that it's on the graph of $y=f(x)$ means $f(3)=4.$ Then, if $x={\color{red}-3},$ we have

$$
f(-x) = f\left(-({\color{red}-3})\right) = f(3) = 4.
$$

 

This means the point $({\color{red}3},4)$ that lies on $y=f(x)$ has a corresponding point $({\color{red}-3},4)$ that lies on $y=f(-x).$

So, for each point on the graph of $y=f(x),$ there will be a point on the graph of $y=f(-x)$ with the *same* $y$-value and the *opposite* $x$-value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=f(-x)[/math]} \\ (-1,2) & (1,2) \\ (0,-1) & (0,-1) \\ (2,0) & (-2,0) \\ (3,4) & (-3,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plot the points and draw the graph of $y = f(-x){:}$

![](images/3a/3ae62ef6496a598d27e485990ab0d3b3cb6f23211de4a015d54614db463bb131.png)

Looking back at the graph, we see that every point on the graph of $y=f(-x)$ is the **reflection across the $y$-axis** of a point on the graph of $y=f(x).$

So, the graph of $y=f(-x)$ can be obtained by reflecting the graph of $y=f(x)$ over the $y$-axis. This result holds in general." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115419 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198592 :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

![](images/34/343917ea041d51cac38619f3577765eee7fbc3ea85e175148b6c591e11ae230b.png)" :question/worked-solution "We compute the three reciprocal trigonometric ratios as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 5 3, \[5pt]
		\sec\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} =  \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac 5 4, \[5pt]
		\cot\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 4 3.
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078399 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-789a361b-1deb-51ca-88a0-26707116d922" "question-9728a2a0-30c7-53d5-836b-39033ca5b896"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078265 :question/worked-solution "Remember that $\sec$ is the reciprocal of $\cos.$ So first we need to compute cosine:

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JL}{KL} = \dfrac{JL}{5}
$$

To find the length $JL,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JL & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{K}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-9} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{JL}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡L & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-4bfcc405-f2a2-5e8e-bff5-6d6acca08903" :question/id #uuid "4bfcc405-f2a2-5e8e-bff5-6d6acca08903" :question/math-academy-id "q-25070" :question/problem "![](images/6e/6eda76bbacb2cbebfe9a798b957c013dc34f684b4d866488541af759b25972b7.png)

$\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that $cot$ is the reciprocal of $tan.$ So first we need to compute tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{PR}{QR}=\frac{3}{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45-9} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1}=2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-db152ebb-c302-5112-8c45-9948cd14ca8b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-db152ebb-c302-5112-8c45-9948cd14ca8b" :answer-field/id #uuid "db152ebb-c302-5112-8c45-9948cd14ca8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-58e41124-d27e-5bf8-a849-55991f19b628" :answer-field/choices ["answer-58e41124-d27e-5bf8-a849-55991f19b628" "answer-bd65e325-f1b8-5c87-9662-6c18254e66f1" "answer-fadee215-c360-5052-9061-2ac46dc7f6ab" "answer-b1098335-0f3d-532a-9ba1-59d86a55f4e4" "answer-f74d244e-220f-5aa8-ba66-446e22db924d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-58e41124-d27e-5bf8-a849-55991f19b628" :answer/id #uuid "58e41124-d27e-5bf8-a849-55991f19b628" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bd65e325-f1b8-5c87-9662-6c18254e66f1" :answer/id #uuid "bd65e325-f1b8-5c87-9662-6c18254e66f1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fadee215-c360-5052-9061-2ac46dc7f6ab" :answer/id #uuid "fadee215-c360-5052-9061-2ac46dc7f6ab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1098335-0f3d-532a-9ba1-59d86a55f4e4" :answer/id #uuid "b1098335-0f3d-532a-9ba1-59d86a55f4e4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f74d244e-220f-5aa8-ba66-446e22db924d" :answer/id #uuid "f74d244e-220f-5aa8-ba66-446e22db924d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-9728a2a0-30c7-53d5-836b-39033ca5b896" :question/id #uuid "9728a2a0-30c7-53d5-836b-39033ca5b896" :question/math-academy-id "q-122902" :question/problem "![](images/a9/a9003434f721485b5ee3eb2ed417d0c4c68514b98060f6149bc974270e55411a.png)

$\operatorname{csc}⁡P=$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that $csc$ is the reciprocal of $sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡P=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{QR}{15}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{R}^{2}-P{Q}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{15}^{2}-{9}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{225-81} \\  & =\sqrt{144} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡P=\frac{QR}{15}=\frac{12}{15}=\frac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡P={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-42169019-4c90-5f92-9ed4-0e9272ff36d7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-42169019-4c90-5f92-9ed4-0e9272ff36d7" :answer-field/id #uuid "42169019-4c90-5f92-9ed4-0e9272ff36d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-9579f35d-0a62-56c0-87be-1dce6c45f688" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fdf065d6-21d7-507f-b607-cc7b49b70a85" "answer-38ae8a7e-8879-58a2-b77d-2f1efa7ea909" "answer-9579f35d-0a62-56c0-87be-1dce6c45f688" "answer-1f66b5f8-e76f-5f77-8f96-098a448df87a" "answer-22e0ee74-658c-52fe-a2b1-2df54d380881"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fdf065d6-21d7-507f-b607-cc7b49b70a85" :answer/id #uuid "fdf065d6-21d7-507f-b607-cc7b49b70a85" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{12}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-38ae8a7e-8879-58a2-b77d-2f1efa7ea909" :answer/id #uuid "38ae8a7e-8879-58a2-b77d-2f1efa7ea909" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{15}{7}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9579f35d-0a62-56c0-87be-1dce6c45f688" :answer/id #uuid "9579f35d-0a62-56c0-87be-1dce6c45f688" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f66b5f8-e76f-5f77-8f96-098a448df87a" :answer/id #uuid "1f66b5f8-e76f-5f77-8f96-098a448df87a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-22e0ee74-658c-52fe-a2b1-2df54d380881" :answer/id #uuid "22e0ee74-658c-52fe-a2b1-2df54d380881" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079643 :tutorial/content "The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

- The reciprocal of **sine** is **cosecant**, abbreviated $\csc.$

$$
\csc(\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\sin(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **cosine** is **secant**, abbreviated $\sec.$

$$
\sec (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\cos(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **tangent** is **cotangent**, abbreviated $\cot.$

$$
\cot (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

Let's write down expressions for $\csc(B),$ $\sec(B),$ and $\cot(B)$ for the triangle below.

![](images/e9/e98dcc332739ff381e8dc43160a907e471062c5b8a75567ba7dbb8687c008efa.png)

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac c b \[5pt]
		\sec(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac c a \[5pt]
		\cot(B) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac a b \
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186079644 :tutorial/content "If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios $\sec,$ $\csc,$ or $\cot$ when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

The trick here is the same that we use for finding $\sin,$ $\cos,$ or $\tan\mathbin{:}$ we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

To illustrate, let's calculate $\csc L$  in the triangle below. 

![](images/9f/9f2e4ea4922783c84a6cb59c5e1532b726d46c9a837a5b1eaa203bbdc6cc1741.png)

Remember that $\csc$ is the reciprocal of $\sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}
$$

To find the length $JK,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16-9} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡L & ={(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}\cdot \sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186078641 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186060376 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

#uuid "dba16e2f-f755-5c6f-b25b-801d348b9282" :question/math-academy-id "q-67435" :question/problem "Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{-4}) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-746714c2-cc0f-5a43-9606-b934d8793273"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186174135] {:db/id 17592186416111 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/b9/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176485 :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186387706 :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

$$
3 \cdot 9 = 27 \: \textrm{cm}.
$$

The empty space in the carton is a rectangular prism that is $9\:\textrm{cm}$ long, $9\:\textrm{cm}$ wide, and $27 - 9 = 18\:\textrm{cm}$ high.

$$
V = lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad w=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad h=18\,\textrm{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$

$$

$$
V=lwh,
$$

The diagram above shows a cubic gas tank. One-fifth of the volume of the tank is filled with gas. If the fuel costs $$0.0016$ per cubic centimeter, how much would it cost to fill the tank to capacity?" :question/worked-solution "The length of $7\,\text{cm}$ shown in the diagram represents one-fifth of the tank's side length. Therefore, the length of each side of the tank is

$$
5\cdot 7=35\,\text{cm}.
$$

The empty space in the cube is a rectangular prism that is $35\,\text{cm}$ long, $35\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $35-7=28\,\text{cm}$ high.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=35\,\text{cm},\,w=35\,\text{cm},\,h=28\,\text{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=35\cdot 35\cdot 28=34\,300\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, to fill the tank to capacity, it would cost

Using the shell method, find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.

![](images/16/16a30b8310128aa588b3278b5a0984193ce57cbb5ea9118fc167a636487363b8.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=2-y^2$ and $g(y)=y.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 2-{y}^{2} & =y \\ {y}^{2}+y-2 & =0 \\ (y+2)(y-1) & =0 \\ y & =-2,1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/f6/f69e2c1cd3b099a4ba192357db32274867c4f296e2c34e31e5110ee31b270317.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=y,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=2-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([2-{y}^{2}]-[y])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2-y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175968 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f03e4c2d-a256-544b-8a7f-59a90059d73b" "question-e40037f0-3304-53a5-a4f4-7220f338664f" "question-1404f19f-22e0-51b4-954a-73312901eafa" "question-1e2fc7b4-11f3-5f1c-807e-b40bd8df74a7" "question-efbcafae-ea63-52c2-855e-a9cfa22be6a8"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175818 :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=3y-y^2$ and $x=y,$  as shown below. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.

![](images/7e/7eca2a7eecfb9555a7e1555555a6d7b435a794e5715537d4fe94998ef00d124a.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=3y-y^2$ and $g(y)=y.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 3y-{y}^{2} & =y \\ 2y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(2-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions corresponding to our region are $y=0$ and $y=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/86/861a1300845e3832a201dd00410d462350f33a4654332b6b6fa7140dc6476dbb.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=y,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=3y-y^2.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y([3y-{y}^{2}]-[y])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(2y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (2{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({2\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{2}) \\  & =2\pi (2(\frac{8}{3}-0)-(\frac{16}{4}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{16}{3}-4) \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1ede84af-72eb-557a-81fe-42dab11d2478" :question/id #uuid "1ede84af-72eb-557a-81fe-42dab11d2478" :question/math-academy-id "q-107218" :question/problem "![](images/89/8957a7db313379597a21e6b51d6c4493058af207a2d8edd5fafb8e549ba45aae.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=1+y$ and $x=1+{y}^{3},$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=1+y$ and $g(y)=1+{y}^{3}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1+y & =1+{y}^{3} \\ y-{y}^{3} & =0 \\ y(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y(1-y)(1+y) & =0 \\ y & =-1,0,1\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions corresponding to our region are $y=0$ and $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/b9/b91dedd1282ce1e9d8546bc6f7c52eba8741a2cd49613a03ef62866a9ba91b0c.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=1+{y}^{3},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1+y.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1+y]-[1+{y}^{3}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(y-{y}^{3})\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-48b6c840-af69-50a7-90ae-fcfa0390abc1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=1+2y-{y}^{2}$ and $x=2y,$ as shown above. Find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=1+2y-{y}^{2}$ and $g(y)=2y.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1+2y-{y}^{2} & =2y \\ 1-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ (1-y)(1+y) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/d9/d9f7cf87c59b7a0fc9600178795524f35a72b12466385e63eafa35c1fdb3537c.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=2y,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1+2y-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1+2y-{y}^{2}]-[2y])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(1+2y-{y}^{2}-2y)\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(1-{y}^{2})\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b7ab163e-5d5d-5698-b7ab-03eea7c74f9e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b7ab163e-5d5d-5698-b7ab-03eea7c74f9e" :answer-field/id #uuid "b7ab163e-5d5d-5698-b7ab-03eea7c74f9e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6f3a483b-b14e-5eaf-a6fa-5d488f2042e5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-fc9016d5-be3d-5277-aaaf-8658739447a8" "answer-139fc7af-0867-5a86-940c-8281935a937b" "answer-6f3a483b-b14e-5eaf-a6fa-5d488f2042e5" "answer-a5fa5ee1-55ae-551e-b55c-cb55db8dd6f5" "answer-2f7b25f4-6ce8-527a-8907-b4e941ca805d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fc9016d5-be3d-5277-aaaf-8658739447a8" :answer/id #uuid "fc9016d5-be3d-5277-aaaf-8658739447a8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(1+4y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-139fc7af-0867-5a86-940c-8281935a937b" :answer/id #uuid "139fc7af-0867-5a86-940c-8281935a937b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(1-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f3a483b-b14e-5eaf-a6fa-5d488f2042e5" :answer/id #uuid "6f3a483b-b14e-5eaf-a6fa-5d488f2042e5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(1-{y}^{2})\text{d}y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a5fa5ee1-55ae-551e-b55c-cb55db8dd6f5" :answer/id #uuid "a5fa5ee1-55ae-551e-b55c-cb55db8dd6f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(1+{y}^{2})\text{d}y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2f7b25f4-6ce8-527a-8907-b4e941ca805d" :answer/id #uuid "2f7b25f4-6ce8-527a-8907-b4e941ca805d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(4y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176403 :question/problem "![](images/a5/a5a3a246f2ecb4bee6cfc46f34d14b5abc9fcf22ed0d6173ed465bfab2cfeca6.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=7-y-{y}^{2},$ $x=5-{y}^{2},$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Now, let $f(y)=7-y-{y}^{2}$ and $g(y)=5-{y}^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 7-y-{y}^{2} & =5-{y}^{2} \\ 2-y & =0 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/cf/cfb914bf7ed0a0c6b9f784d46a6761cd97c352fcc4e82abb29a72dc12d8ab7ca.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=5-{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=7-y-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y([7-y-{y}^{2}]-[5-{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(2-y)\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (2{\int }_{0}^{2}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({2\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{2}-{\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}) \\  & =2\pi (2(\frac{4}{2}-0)-(\frac{8}{3}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (4-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{8\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9c63fd60-a918-5151-ad1a-213063aeef6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9c63fd60-a918-5151-ad1a-213063aeef6f" :answer-field/id #uuid "9c63fd60-a918-5151-ad1a-213063aeef6f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-6a9bfb4c-8588-57d6-bd1d-a486a788d455" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6a9bfb4c-8588-57d6-bd1d-a486a788d455"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6a9bfb4c-8588-57d6-bd1d-a486a788d455" :answer/id #uuid "6a9bfb4c-8588-57d6-bd1d-a486a788d455" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8\pi}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-e40037f0-3304-53a5-a4f4-7220f338664f" :question/id #uuid "e40037f0-3304-53a5-a4f4-7220f338664f" :question/math-academy-id "q-126377" :question/problem "![](images/48/482781bb21d011df5a9140b2b1fb0ebe1108f746c0055077d4f4e9a91fce735d.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $y=\sqrt{2-x},$ $x={y}^{2},$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the second function in terms $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{2-x} \\ {y}^{2} & =2-x \\ x & =2-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $f(y)={y}^{2}$ and $g(y)=2-{y}^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ {y}^{2} & =2-{y}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=1.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/48/48905a174d688fdb3e099debb7840173a2ce047816003a5be9c089997196f9fb.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=f(y)={y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=g(y)=2-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([2-{y}^{2}]-[{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =4\pi ({\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =4\pi ((\frac{1}{2}-0)-(\frac{1}{4}-0)) \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0ac10175-16bb-5872-9c8f-0de12b255415"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0ac10175-16bb-5872-9c8f-0de12b255415" :answer-field/id #uuid "0ac10175-16bb-5872-9c8f-0de12b255415" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-36e02b44-a709-533e-8923-9cd6635295c8" :answer-field/choices ["answer-96c8069d-b163-5345-aa21-42e30dfc170b" "answer-0bdd21a9-b33a-5551-894f-eefc01cd484b" "answer-dd29541b-ac6a-5c52-b43d-f88aae4b76d5" "answer-54fb0fe4-d278-59fe-baf1-7676faf2662c" "answer-36e02b44-a709-533e-8923-9cd6635295c8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-96c8069d-b163-5345-aa21-42e30dfc170b" :answer/id #uuid "96c8069d-b163-5345-aa21-42e30dfc170b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0bdd21a9-b33a-5551-894f-eefc01cd484b" :answer/id #uuid "0bdd21a9-b33a-5551-894f-eefc01cd484b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dd29541b-ac6a-5c52-b43d-f88aae4b76d5" :answer/id #uuid "dd29541b-ac6a-5c52-b43d-f88aae4b76d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-54fb0fe4-d278-59fe-baf1-7676faf2662c" :answer/id #uuid "54fb0fe4-d278-59fe-baf1-7676faf2662c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-36e02b44-a709-533e-8923-9cd6635295c8" :answer/id #uuid "36e02b44-a709-533e-8923-9cd6635295c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1404f19f-22e0-51b4-954a-73312901eafa" :question/id #uuid "1404f19f-22e0-51b4-954a-73312901eafa" :question/math-academy-id "q-107142" :question/problem "![](images/92/920aca572a3b6fc828d6c37246b348aa2b017d1bc4e022ea06c12d0fa09ad6ee.png)

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=(1-y)^{2}$ and $y=\sqrt{1-x},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the second function in terms $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{1-x} \\ {y}^{2} & =1-x \\ x & =1-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $f(y)=1-{y}^{2}$ and $g(y)=(1-y)^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1-{y}^{2} & =(1-y)^{2} \\ 1-{y}^{2} & =1-2y+{y}^{2} \\ 2{y}^{2}-2y & =0 \\ 2y(y-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/02/02e6b4204b1edf682dd332e28830dc84aa0e41d3728c66442d777f6fe9daccfc.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=(1-y)^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1-{y}^{2}]-[(1-y)^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y([1-{y}^{2}]-[1-2y+{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y(2y-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =4\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =4\pi ({\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =4\pi ((\frac{1}{3}-0)-(\frac{1}{4}-0)) \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{12}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\end{aligned}

Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=1+y$ and $x=1-2y+{y}^{2},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "First, let $f(y)=1+y$ and $g(y)=1-2y+{y}^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 1+y & =1-2y+{y}^{2} \\ 3y-{y}^{2} & =0 \\ y(3-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,3\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions corresponding to our region are $y=0$ and $y=3.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=3.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/84/84e62b99598649ac48d55171b0d6bf7e5d26e38a6ad94c46ef9c89145e60e29a.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=1-2y+{y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=1+y.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y([1+y]-[1-2y+{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}y(3y-{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(3{y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (3{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({3\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{3}-{\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{3}) \\  & =2\pi (3(\frac{27}{3}-0)-(\frac{81}{4}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (27-\frac{81}{4}) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-410a3349-db09-5c6c-877b-7b43454d7322"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-410a3349-db09-5c6c-877b-7b43454d7322" :answer-field/id #uuid "410a3349-db09-5c6c-877b-7b43454d7322" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1853b3af-28f4-5ef9-aad8-03a6eaf50446" :answer-field/choices ["answer-aedf06dc-11bf-5210-87fb-2324f78a6574" "answer-1853b3af-28f4-5ef9-aad8-03a6eaf50446" "answer-e847bcfd-c659-5ed7-a215-e4e98478c99c" "answer-9ee05a02-1be6-5002-8a40-86020d83d578" "answer-efd08d18-ffa2-5e0a-8532-bcddc6c9bf2c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aedf06dc-11bf-5210-87fb-2324f78a6574" :answer/id #uuid "aedf06dc-11bf-5210-87fb-2324f78a6574" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "9\pi " :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1853b3af-28f4-5ef9-aad8-03a6eaf50446" :answer/id #uuid "1853b3af-28f4-5ef9-aad8-03a6eaf50446" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{27\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e847bcfd-c659-5ed7-a215-e4e98478c99c" :answer/id #uuid "e847bcfd-c659-5ed7-a215-e4e98478c99c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{27\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9ee05a02-1be6-5002-8a40-86020d83d578" :answer/id #uuid "9ee05a02-1be6-5002-8a40-86020d83d578" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{81\pi }{10}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-efd08d18-ffa2-5e0a-8532-bcddc6c9bf2c" :answer/id #uuid "efd08d18-ffa2-5e0a-8532-bcddc6c9bf2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{81\pi }{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-efbcafae-ea63-52c2-855e-a9cfa22be6a8" :question/id #uuid "efbcafae-ea63-52c2-855e-a9cfa22be6a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-352199" :question/problem "![](images/1d/1d8d3dfa1134b7fd5861ff70e493ead2227dd2d322e8436e28a903e0c596a408.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curves $x=4y-{y}^{2},$ $y=\sqrt{x},$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. Calculate the volume $V$ of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the second function in terms of $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{x} \\ x & ={y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let $f(y)=4y-{y}^{2}$ and $g(y)={y}^{2}.$

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ 4y-{y}^{2} & ={y}^{2} \\ 4y-2{y}^{2} & =0 \\ 2y(2-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=2.$ So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2.$ 

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/c5/c5a117e2af85e3380942939812442eac7b899a2259af79ad032654fc5662a767.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)={y}^{2},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=4y-{y}^{2}.$

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =2\pi {\int }_{c}^{d}y([\text{right}]-[\text{left}])\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y([4y-{y}^{2}]-[{y}^{2}])\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}y(4y-2{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(4{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3})\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi (4{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\text{d}y) \\  & =2\pi ({4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{2}-{2\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{2}) \\  & =2\pi (4(\frac{8}{3}-0)-2(\frac{16}{4}-0)) \\  & =2\pi (\frac{32}{3}-8) \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b70140cd-8dd2-5535-a3c9-379587f1fc13"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b70140cd-8dd2-5535-a3c9-379587f1fc13" :answer-field/id #uuid "b70140cd-8dd2-5535-a3c9-379587f1fc13" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7553f952-2b67-5919-b814-110becde50fa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7553f952-2b67-5919-b814-110becde50fa"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7553f952-2b67-5919-b814-110becde50fa" :answer/id #uuid "7553f952-2b67-5919-b814-110becde50fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16\pi}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176983 :tutorial/content "Consider the region enclosed by the curves $x=f(y)$ on the right, $x=g(y)$ on the left, and the horizontal lines $y=c$ and $y=d,$ as shown below. If an inspector comes to inspect the water bottles, what is the probability that they will find an upside down label before checking the $5$th bottle? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of bottles checked until a defect is found. On average, the chance of finding an upside down label on any water bottle is 

$$
p=\frac{20}{1\,000}=0.02.
$$

So, the number of bottles that the inspector checks before finding an upside down label can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success $p=0.02.$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.02).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.02)^{x-1}(0.02) \\  & =(0.98)^{x-1}(0.02)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding an upside down label before checking the $5$th bottle is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & =(0.98)^{1-1}(0.02)+(0.98)^{2-1}(0.02)+(0.98)^{3-1}(0.02)+(0.98)^{4-1}(0.02) \\  & =(0.02)+(0.98)(0.02)+(0.98)^{2}(0.02)+(0.98)^{3}(0.02) \\  & =[1+0.98+(0.98)^{2}+(0.98)^{3}](0.02) \\  & ≈0.078\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186156129 :answer-field/correct 17592186156132 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157315 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-adc9ba22-54ae-50d6-b1c5-428a57977aea"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-adc9ba22-54ae-50d6-b1c5-428a57977aea" :question/id #uuid "adc9ba22-54ae-50d6-b1c5-428a57977aea" :question/math-academy-id "q-85881" :question/problem "An experiment consists of tossing a fair coin until it comes up heads. $$

$$

What is the probability that the first positive test result will be made on the $3$rd test or later?" :question/worked-solution "A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$

$$

Let $X$ be the number of inhabitants checked until the first infected patient is found. Since the chance of a single patient being infected is $30%,$ the number of inhabitants checked until the first infected patient is found can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=30%=\frac{30}{100}=0.3.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.3).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.3)^{x-1}(0.3) \\  & =(0.7)^{x-1}(0.3)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X\ge 3),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X\ge 3)=1-P(X<3)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<3) & =P(X\in \{1,2\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(0.7)^{1-1}(0.3)+(0.7)^{2-1}(0.3) \\  & =(0.3)+(0.7)(0.3) \\  & =[1+0.7](0.3) \\  & =0.51.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding the first positive patient on the $3$rd test or later is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3) & =1-P(X<3) \\  & =1-0.51 \\  & =0.49.\end{aligned}

On average, the team has a $20%$ chance of losing each game. What is the probability that the team plays at least $4$ games without losing (i.e., the first loss occurs after the $4$th game)?" :question/worked-solution "A geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(1-p)^{x-1}p
$$

Let $X$ be the number of games played until they lose their first game. Since the chance of losing each game is $20%,$ the number of games played before the team loses can be modeled as a geometric random variable with a probability of success

$$
p=20%=\frac{20}{100}=0.2.
$$

So, $X∼\text{Geom}(0.2).$ In this case, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(1-0.2)^{x-1}(0.2) \\  & =(0.8)^{x-1}(0.2)\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $P(X>4),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X>4)=1-P(X\le 4)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 4) & =P(X\in \{1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & =(0.8)^{1-1}(0.2)+(0.8)^{2-1}(0.2)+(0.8)^{3-1}(0.2)+(0.8)^{4-1}(0.2) \\  & =(0.2)+(0.8)(0.2)+(0.8)^{2}(0.2)+(0.8)^{3}(0.2) \\  & =[1+0.8+(0.8)^{2}+(0.8)^{3}](0.2) \\  & =0.5904.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that the team will play at least $4$ games before their first loss

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>4) & =1-P(X\le 4) \\  & =1-0.5904 \\  & =0.4096.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f5a73d02-83b1-5576-b29f-c152341639c1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\  & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205341 :answer-field/correct "answer-cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-86d96929-a573-5ba1-a568-15337e2bcf56" "answer-cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" "answer-ff114911-6bea-5d83-a4a0-4820ac877a2b" "answer-e136544d-ec3c-563b-b13e-653feae14454" "answer-0288d1c8-90da-55c4-98e8-5a5eabefe8cc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86d96929-a573-5ba1-a568-15337e2bcf56" :answer/id #uuid "86d96929-a573-5ba1-a568-15337e2bcf56" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-7 & -29\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" :answer/id #uuid "cc83261d-2254-5227-8497-098b5fbcaed7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ff114911-6bea-5d83-a4a0-4820ac877a2b" :answer/id #uuid "ff114911-6bea-5d83-a4a0-4820ac877a2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}25 \\ -11\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e136544d-ec3c-563b-b13e-653feae14454" :answer/id #uuid "e136544d-ec3c-563b-b13e-653feae14454" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 & 22\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0288d1c8-90da-55c4-98e8-5a5eabefe8cc" :answer/id #uuid "0288d1c8-90da-55c4-98e8-5a5eabefe8cc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 22\end{aligned}]" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-3f634cb0-d91f-55a0-8036-9bf4e6795f5f" :question/id #uuid "3f634cb0-d91f-55a0-8036-9bf4e6795f5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-269525" :question/problem "Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c4950606-28b0-554b-95e7-9a39d66b5c16" "answer-field-5f8172f4-c9fe-5e8d-b6a6-b70f7a350883"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c4950606-28b0-554b-95e7-9a39d66b5c16" :answer-field/id #uuid "c4950606-28b0-554b-95e7-9a39d66b5c16" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-85a4f0d1-a936-5ab3-bd96-2206322e6e46" :answer-field/choices ["answer-85a4f0d1-a936-5ab3-bd96-2206322e6e46"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85a4f0d1-a936-5ab3-bd96-2206322e6e46" :answer/id #uuid "85a4f0d1-a936-5ab3-bd96-2206322e6e46" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5f8172f4-c9fe-5e8d-b6a6-b70f7a350883" :answer-field/id #uuid "5f8172f4-c9fe-5e8d-b6a6-b70f7a350883" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-45292744-8b9c-5c5e-b27f-372a2cae9e71" :answer-field/choices ["answer-45292744-8b9c-5c5e-b27f-372a2cae9e71"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-45292744-8b9c-5c5e-b27f-372a2cae9e71" :answer/id #uuid "45292744-8b9c-5c5e-b27f-372a2cae9e71" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8b961be3-a61d-5fd5-a33f-daa3b859082d" :question/id #uuid "8b961be3-a61d-5fd5-a33f-daa3b859082d" :question/math-academy-id "q-276044" :question/problem "Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by

$$

$$

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}
$$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{n}{n!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{(-1)^{6}\cdot 6}{6!}|=\frac{6}{720}=\frac{1}{120}.
$$

 

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{120}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186099963 :answer-field/correct 17592186099965 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100925 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-aa9e57c4-993f-58af-8f8c-2c21d29224b2" "question-bb487298-b519-5edb-8e52-6ad72f9356fb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-aa9e57c4-993f-58af-8f8c-2c21d29224b2" :question/id #uuid "aa9e57c4-993f-58af-8f8c-2c21d29224b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-83612" :question/problem "Given that

$$

$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}-1}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{(i+1)^{2}-1}| & \le 0.1 \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i+1-1} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ {i}^{2}+2i & \ge 10.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

We substitute $a=2$ and $b=-12$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry. This gives

$$

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-1$ and $b=4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{4}{2(-1)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(-2)} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=2.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we can substitute $x=2$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}+4x+1 \\  & =-(2)^{2}+4(2)+1 \\  & =-4+8+1 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(2,5).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186083188 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c9db5029-028a-58a7-87ff-11b09d5541ba" "question-f5ac6aea-bcfe-5a0e-83c5-58a351f6e0ff"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186082944 :question/problem "The axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=0.25x^2+kx+2$ is $x=-6.$ Find the value of $k.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k.$ Then, we will set our result equal to $-6.$

$$

Substituting $a=0.25$ and $b=k$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{k}{2(0.25)} \\  & =-\frac{k}{0.5} \\  & =-2k.\end{aligned}

We already know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-6,$ so we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2k & =-6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}

$$

Suppose we want to find the axis of symmetry of the function $y=3x^2-6x+1.$ To do this, we substitute $a=3$ and $b=-6$ into the above formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a} \\  & =-\frac{(-6)}{2(3)} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=1$ is the equation of the axis of symmetry. 

![](images/88/88ee917eb387ee60e67080785519ffe9cb4333adcd602a733659d0447c37f61a.png)

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so $x=1$ also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we can substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3{x}^{2}-6x+1 \\  & =3(1)^{2}-6(1)+1 \\  & =3-6+1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-2).$

<table align="center" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="35px" rowspan="2" width="30px">${∇}_{x,z}({∇}_{x,z}f)=\text{ }$</td>
<td align="center" height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="35px"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the variable subset gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,z}\,f & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz) \\ \frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}yz \\ xy\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $x$ and $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{∂}{∂x}(yz)=0\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(yz)=y \\  & \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(xy)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,z}({∇}_{x,z}\,f) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & y \\ y & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b586955b-6ca9-5533-8861-e70a511d63db" "answer-field-29c11c41-4251-59f9-a07b-6dd2357b05fe" $f(x;w)={w}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2},$ compute ${∇}_{w}({∇}_{w}\,f).$

<table align="center" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="35px" rowspan="2" width="30px">${∇}_{w}({∇}_{w}\,f)=\text{ }$</td>
<td align="center" height="30px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">$2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1})$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center" height="35px"></td>
<td align="center">$2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1})$</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "First, we compute ${∇}_{w}\,f$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{1}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{1}}({w}_{1}{x}_{1}-{w}_{2}{x}_{2})^{2}=2{w}_{2}{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂{w}_{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{w}_{2}}({w}_{1}{x}_{1}-{w}_{2}{x}_{2})^{2}=({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{1}^{2}}=2{w}_{2}{x}_{2}^{2}\,\, &  & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{1}∂{w}_{2}}=2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\  & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{2}∂{w}_{1}}=2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1})\,\, &  & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{2}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{w}({∇}_{w}\,f) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{1}∂{w}_{2}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{2}∂{w}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{w}_{2}^{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{w}_{2}{x}_{2}^{2} & 2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) \\ 2{x}_{2}({w}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}) & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eaa3fc51-52ac-520e-88d7-534ea602e135" "answer-field-a75257c9-8063-572f-b90b-975bf7853ddd"] :db/ensure - The shape $R$ is a rhombus. Therefore, it has two pairs of congruent sides that are adjacent to each other, so it is a kite.

- The shape $S$ is a parallelogram. Any two adjacent sides are not congruent with each other, therefore, it is not a kite.

![](images/1d/1dbe4c3e8ea97c0ac077c37143802366c5817d86965ab1dbc5abf54cd01d27c3.png)

Remember that a rectangle is a quadrilateral where all angles are right with two pairs of parallel sides.

With that in mind, let's look at each shape in turn.

- The shape $P$ is an isosceles trapezoid. It has no right angles, therefore, it is not a rectangle.

:question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(y-x)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}
