:question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262710 :question/id #uuid "9c13e73f-8b16-5eac-90ca-cc2a4f61af68" :question/math-academy-id "q-127080"} {:db/id 17592186262715 :question/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262718 :question/id #uuid "bf94cd2c-9106-5cc5-9f8f-bee0a724f45f" :question/math-academy-id "q-127145"} {:db/id 17592186262719 :question/id #uuid $$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $4,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-x=1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x-y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0-12t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(0-0)-12(2\pi -0) \\  & =-24\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262720 :question/id #uuid "4b077b66-1e99-5133-b08d-623645791b05" :question/math-academy-id "q-127148"} {:db/id 17592186262721 :question/id #uuid :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"}] :question/problem "![](images/6e/6eebbc5ae9f548f5b00de9a12d454fa788884bf73ad46a1065eab0d26330a921.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/2b/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180038 :question/id #uuid "e0b1aae8-7058-5a37-a641-ca7e8583e806" :question/math-academy-id "q-126940" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179746 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a9ea5a-dcc8-51ed-90bc-dd684ef71ca9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "153220d6-7689-5056-8b5b-6d10695accb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186260060} {:answer/id #uuid "39ef2d5d-86ef-5bc0-a9ec-82673d7b7699" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186260393} {:answer/id #uuid "7523559d-4e43-59f2-bd01-34c48fcecddf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186260899} {:answer/id #uuid "9f78043b-d21c-5406-8dbe-ff8fab366365" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186261259} {:answer/id #uuid "cfe74df2-842d-5ac2-840e-8b0249def4b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186261711}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "153220d6-7689-5056-8b5b-6d10695accb9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186260060} :answer-field/id #uuid "e164db38-546a-5334-8c07-335889e10d58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262518}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/c7/c71395cfe5877546509f24656ba23f0883cbd3ee8c145c10abae9600c8bd5c4a.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/e9/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180039 :question/id #uuid "72bfedb9-24a7-5361-9689-9e032cb56805" :question/math-academy-id "q-126943"} {:db/id 17592186262722 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/85/85b4da8c0fa35867871b6254ba20f505b7596f2c97226adb2ed01339fe4cbedf.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=5{e}^{-x}\,i+4\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,e],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](images/55/559bbc20aa7d47eaad47a8975f80c8efb91bd03bc816357bc6047675dc755c9b.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =5{e}^{-x}=5{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\frac{5}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{5}{t})\cdot (1)-(4)\cdot (\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262738 :question/id #uuid "d7df129a-7685-5a03-8c7b-340092011e9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127233"} {:db/id 17592186262739 :question/id #uuid "b74be94c-a6f2-5d0a-8660-699d2ff2d45b" :question/math-academy-id "q-127244"} {:db/id 17592186262740 :question/id #uuid "42dae85e-af3c-52f4-a342-edbfb5509ac9" :question/math-academy-id "q-127253" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179746 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a9ea5a-dcc8-51ed-90bc-dd684ef71ca9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14506f23-b7d1-50e2-b7d6-575d362006d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186260054} {:answer/id #uuid "c9aa7ce3-f49a-53f5-8930-c62b6d6c8760" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186261659} {:answer/id #uuid "ecd35a62-5758-5dfb-8a79-58eaad86d417" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261954} {:answer/id #uuid "f5c6fb02-0c1a-52ca-8814-4034572247cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186262025} {:answer/id #uuid "fde5bf23-2aa5-5f61-aed8-c77dfd32c840" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186262101}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "f5c6fb02-0c1a-52ca-8814-4034572247cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186262025} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ffccb8a-a39d-5a7a-a89e-228e3ce4f2c6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262209}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/cd/cd21413d8eea5e2fec67eebe22967c846fd7916fd4fb0fbe5f8efe7ac9df6b1a.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y=1-x$ from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=1-t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/e2/e288ed1095be61e4645fb63c22b7fd2cb605d34795c30557e84afb31b7ec8721.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1)\cdot (-1)-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2-0 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262741 :question/id #uuid "6e7eff5f-8b84-5752-bf2b-9206857b0d37" :question/math-academy-id "q-127254" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179746 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a9ea5a-dcc8-51ed-90bc-dd684ef71ca9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62235db6-575c-58cc-9ea4-bb528398093e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186260721} {:answer/id #uuid "7a8d5f64-67d3-5dce-8551-9f910cdef724" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186260944} {:answer/id #uuid "dc023b88-e9da-5465-abd7-a53791e497db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186261823} {:answer/id #uuid "edf8fb76-10ab-53d9-a7da-5af08b0f7758" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186261967} {:answer/id #uuid "faea5b08-5f3d-5e20-a75e-e18c259cc4db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186262070}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "edf8fb76-10ab-53d9-a7da-5af08b0f7758" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186261967} :answer-field/id #uuid "afced7f6-385b-5b50-b3de-6f71c6df96dc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186262439}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/67/67dca8f0202d0c5d1041935a6aee7c4ebd0e3c6c449f2ee1a5ff24c1f381410c.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/08/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above." :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186421764 :question/id #uuid "ddff35a9-8792-529b-9827-d26481dbe529" :question/math-academy-id "q-127235"} {:db/id 17592186050224} {:db/id 17592186050694} {:answer-field/choices {:db/id 17592186180509}} {:db/id 17592186180506 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180725 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Calculating flux using this definition is often cumbersome because we need to calculate $\mathbf n,$ the outward-pointing unit normal vector. 

In practice, we often use the following alternative formula to calculate the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

We'll derive this formula at the end of the lesson.

**Watch Out!** When applying this formula, we must choose a positively-oriented parameterization for $C.$ This formula will *not* work if $C$ is negatively oriented!" :tutorial/id #uuid "c74e835b-f210-5a77-8d6e-aef474c89522" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5851 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cb889341-22d5-52e6-9979-1fd814bc5cec" :step/math-academy-id 35829 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180504}} {:db/id 17592186180507 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179746 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179608 :question/id #uuid "337d9d7e-5488-5e6d-af34-e01d22d3d0b9" :question/math-academy-id "e-9574"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83a9ea5a-dcc8-51ed-90bc-dd684ef71ca9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180038} {:db/id 17592186180039} {:db/id 17592186262722} {:db/id 17592186262723} {:db/id 17592186262734} {:db/id 17592186262735} {:db/id 17592186262738} {:db/id 17592186262739} {:db/id 17592186262740} {:db/id 17592186262741} {:db/id 17592186362552} {:db/id 17592186421761} {:db/id 17592186421764}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve"} :step/id #uuid "f9195b98-bf60-5d80-a9f1-4dbe4c7ec614" :step/math-academy-id 35863 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180510}} {:db/id 17592186180509 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180727 :tutorial/content "As we've seen, the flux of a vector field $\mathbf F$ through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve $C$ is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ 

The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

- In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is unique at every point on $C.$

- However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between *two* normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

![](images/d1/d193eb8109ead15de50c06a7bb0b654243173d882bd361f9fd34026aa23c1b5f.png)

Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction. 

For example, for the vector field $\mathbf F$ and curve $C$ below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

![](images/4f/4f92dd5334b5836703857c081049f126d39c141e84d8e94171e338a162cf3cc4.png)

Finally, to calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across a non-closed curve $C,$ we can continue to use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

**Watch Out!** To apply this formula, we usually need to parameterize $C.$ It is *vital* that we pick a parameterization where the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is a $90^\circ$ *clockwise* rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2794e26-620d-59e9-85de-a3bb49f6991a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5869 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves"} :step/id #uuid "c6cc7967-4281-527a-8021-7768a792728f" :step/math-academy-id 35901 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180507}} {:db/id 17592186180510 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180728 :tutorial/content "Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

First, recall that if $C$ is parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then 

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},
$$

where it is assumed that $C$ is positively-oriented. 

Substituting our expression for $\mathbf n$ into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that $\textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||})||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}})\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot ({y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P(x(t),y(t)){y}^{′}(t)-Q(x(t),y(t)){x}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cc71a06d-4832-5949-91b4-71cb0f8185ca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5870 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Main Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7543ee2e-ca36-5209-8a6f-1fae02154a3d" :step/math-academy-id 35902}] :activity/title "Calculating Flux in Two-Dimensional Vector Fields" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179867} {:db/id 17592186180506 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180725 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. $$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n},\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{x}_{i}=250,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{y}_{i}=265, \\  & {\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{x}_{i}^{2}=3\,460,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{y}_{i}^{2}=5\,720.\end{aligned}
$$

${S}_{xx}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data ${x}_{i}$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}{({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given statistics in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & =3\,460-\frac{1}{25}(250)^{2} \\  & =3\,460-2\,500 \\  & =960.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186204455 :question/id #uuid "d73c45cf-d35a-5a29-81ab-7afc1b61c919" :question/math-academy-id "q-251897"} {:db/id 17592186512885 :question/id #uuid "42fccfda-10de-5970-a9ed-3564137d6e6d" :question/math-academy-id "q-251893"} {:db/id 17592186512907 :question/id #uuid "8985aab7-37e2-5eaf-8405-71a24796c1c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-251895"} {:db/id 17592186512942 :question/id #uuid "d18e628f-0f71-500f-a909-b31e50aba9f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-251899"} {:db/id 17592186512955 :question/id #uuid "f69f9435-629a-5550-ae7c-8e46c05363dd" :question/math-academy-id "q-251891"} {:db/id 17592186521471 :question/id #uuid "26b0163b-edde-5aab-b2bd-a06d38a87337" :question/math-academy-id "q-251898" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "66aa0cf4-9fdd-5d95-be6b-811b502b95a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{S}_{yy}=22" :db/id 17592186520998} {:answer/id #uuid "8f3ad138-0924-5a40-8f81-cbba162c0f19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{S}_{yy}=16" :db/id 17592186521088} {:answer/id #uuid "b647c1b2-e8a2-513d-bca8-1ba7556ab769" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{S}_{yy}=21.3" :db/id 17592186521170} {:answer/id #uuid "ba06e549-bfbb-5699-a72e-3e553bcf6f6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{S}_{yy}=13" :db/id 17592186521178} {:answer/id #uuid "f4353feb-c770-5137-9c93-96535a82b4a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{S}_{yy}=19" :db/id 17592186521299}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186521088} :answer-field/id #uuid "97de8c2b-2160-5c30-92a5-23ff5b28889c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186521400}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the two sets of $8$ paired observations shown in the table below.

$$
\sigma_x^2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

where $\overline x$ is the mean of $x.$ 

The summation term

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

is known as a **sum of squares** and is denoted $S_{xx}.$ As we'll see, this quantity often appears in statistical analysis, so giving it a separate notation is useful.

Similarly, if we have a data set $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n,$ then we define

$$
S_{yy} =  \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \overline y)^2.
$$

Now, suppose we have the bivariate data set

$$
(x_1, y_1), \qquad (x_2, y_2),\qquad \ldots, \qquad (x_n, y_n).
$$

Then, the covariance is given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)(y_i - \overline y)
$$

and we may define $S_{xy}$ as

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}).
$$

Finally, we can define the variance and covariance in terms of $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{x}^{2} & =\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n},\,{\sigma }_{y}^{2}=\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n},\,\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7e454c5-fb32-5adc-b4bd-0eb93ccd4ce7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10575 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "780a886e-f7ec-5134-8c19-6ef13b7e6958" :step/math-academy-id 226927 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204876}} {:db/id 17592186204876 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203803 :question/id #uuid "6f0e3d4b-943b-5710-a996-ac4d3c68778d" :question/math-academy-id "e-16399"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d0afa4d8-6d02-52c6-9836-12089de8f406" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048914} {:db/id 17592186049126}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204443} {:db/id 17592186204444} {:db/id 17592186512866} {:db/id 17592186512868} {:db/id 17592186512914} {:db/id 17592186536828} {:db/id 17592186536892}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Sums of Squares Given a Dataset or Summary Statistics"} :step/id #uuid "c4508f2d-5b01-5156-a636-efc40f9518ac" :step/math-academy-id 226928 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204877}} {:db/id 17592186204877 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204009 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203805 :question/id #uuid "7daa2313-4672-5624-aac2-e3b87b6ec366" :question/math-academy-id "e-16401"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "714000f9-caea-57a3-a8cb-6b8ec99960d1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204447} {:db/id 17592186204448} {:db/id 17592186512890} {:db/id 17592186512901} {:db/id 17592186512920} {:db/id 17592186512923} {:db/id 17592186521455} {:db/id 17592186521460}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Variance and Covariance"} :step/id #uuid "b96fcd87-a442-5e10-907a-17ae7bf45eef" :step/math-academy-id 226931 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204878}} {:db/id 17592186204878 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205126 :tutorial/content "Calculating $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ using their definitions can be cumbersome. ![](images/78/78416d3c8ec8a8351ecfe0a4ea81feb05cce29f55dd9ec4bc676e6363dd49ec0.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of cosine:

$$
\cos L = \dfrac {\textrm{adjacent}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {JL}{KL} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $KL$. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned} KL &= \sqrt{JK^2 + JL^2} \\ &= \sqrt{(3)^2 + (3\sqrt3)^2} \\ &= \sqrt{9 + 27} \\ &= \sqrt{36} \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](images/e0/e0fb47c85d56c314389a0a334029b3b769f13ddcca6ab15a9021cf6361e4b1ce.png)" :question/worked-solution "Recall the definition of sine:

$$
\sin Y = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {XZ}{YZ} = \dfrac{XZ}{61}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XZ$. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned} XZ &= \sqrt{YZ^2 - XY^2} \\ &= \sqrt{61^2 - 60^2} \\ &= \sqrt{3721- 3600} \\ &= \sqrt{121} \\ &= 11 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned} \sin Y&= \dfrac{XZ}{61} = \dfrac{11}{61}. \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078736 :question/id #uuid "c1e75dc5-f772-58f9-854d-88ee9165b21b" :question/math-academy-id "q-14580"} {:db/id 17592186078737 :question/id #uuid "a297f665-c83d-57c5-a5b3-4e4cdbf2c7d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-14581"} {:db/id 17592186234385 :question/id #uuid "021c99cd-4ec5-510e-b0c7-e32ccd554ad9" :question/math-academy-id "q-76560" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186078393 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0a83e174-ab83-5bf6-898e-0fe5cddc8ef4" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem to Solve for a Leg"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "In a right triangle $△XYZ,$ $∠X$ is a right angle, $XZ=\sqrt{5}$ and $YZ=7.$ Find the cosine of $∠Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/ea/ea0502e8b261358c7b55c60df02474c5b39a75cbb104d6ba3efb40300294ef56.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{7}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{7}^{2}-(\sqrt{5})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49-5} \\  & =\sqrt{44} \\  & =2\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}Y & =\frac{XY}{7}=\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078394 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078254 :question/id #uuid "cc59ecc0-e886-5e7d-8fbe-c63df5995d3d" :question/math-academy-id "e-3246"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7dc4cb42-6295-5484-b37e-0c557c4f6073" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186078740 :question/id #uuid "5ae01ab6-b771-5f83-a86c-608699d71684" :question/math-academy-id "q-14644"} {:db/id 17592186079166 :question/id #uuid "4e720463-1cf7-54ea-95e2-cbfc8b2723ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-65359"}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem with Decimals"} {:db/id 17592186078254 :question/id #uuid "cc59ecc0-e886-5e7d-8fbe-c63df5995d3d" :question/math-academy-id "e-3246" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186078394 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7dc4cb42-6295-5484-b37e-0c557c4f6073" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem with Decimals"}] :question/problem "Calculate $\tan K$.

$$
\tan K = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{adjacent}} = \dfrac {JL}{JK} = \dfrac{JL}{7.5}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned} JL &= \sqrt{KL^2 - JK^2} \\ &= \sqrt{12.5^2 - 7.5^2} \\ &= \sqrt{156.25-56.25} \\ &= \sqrt{100} \\ &= 10 \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned} \tan K&= \dfrac{JL}{7.5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{10}{7.5} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac 4 3. \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078740 :question/id #uuid "5ae01ab6-b771-5f83-a86c-608699d71684" :question/math-academy-id "q-14644" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186078394 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7dc4cb42-6295-5484-b37e-0c557c4f6073" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem with Decimals"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9aa19083-4794-58ee-8fad-4ca0e69496d1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{12}{5}" :db/id 17592186075317} {:answer/id #uuid "dc53aa94-495a-5de2-ac52-713c00c8250d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{13}{12}" :db/id 17592186075318} {:answer/id #uuid "dfbd7e1a-d670-5049-be73-b31bceca763c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{12}" :db/id 17592186075319} {:answer/id #uuid "e7eb01b0-bbd4-5b07-a9a3-831c67740f92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{12}{13}" :db/id 17592186075320} {:answer/id #uuid "56ab04b7-2119-5221-9469-344254399a8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{13}" :db/id 17592186075321}] :answer-field/id #uuid "26d5018e-19d4-5b5f-aa3f-04252b407275" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186075316}] :question/problem "![](images/f9/f9f59d4328ad43e6e342da3cf9e87ccd5dfe33b97c46424e7fcc2b9f562fc452.png)

How can we find the value $\sin \theta$ if we don't know one of the relevant sides?

![](images/ae/ae5157e6824fd98861194302ab912e76d9e79dade6706dfbedea97d859f18a79.png)

Recall the definition of sine:

$$
\sin \theta = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {AC}{AB} = \dfrac 1 c
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $c$. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c &= \sqrt{AC^{2} + BC^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{1^{2} + 1^{2}} \\
&= \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can finish computing the value of $\sin\theta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin θ &= \frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1 \cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

No matter which trigonometric function we need to find, if we are missing one of the relevant sides but we know the lengths of the other two sides, we can always use the Pythagorean Theorem." "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=25.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $5$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{xy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{5}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129756 :question/id #uuid "5e21b1a1-dd1a-5b1e-a6f4-aca8044792b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-40073" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6aa22172-aed4-5605-92ab-59f3b9c082a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186375137} {:answer/id #uuid "47674ef2-eb40-5ead-b7da-b61decf7c865" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{9}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186375138} {:answer/id #uuid "a76f3460-fc95-508d-924f-bca258671c28" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186375139} {:answer/id #uuid "8f0a05b0-be97-5bf2-ae2d-2d653d7ac4e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186375140} {:answer/id #uuid "6976b7cc-768c-59b4-88b8-9e266d9b514a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186375141}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186375141} :answer-field/id #uuid "7d1c327d-1302-5a46-953f-a8e3268dd875" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186375136}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)^{2}\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

$$

"![](images/4d/4d2a71ffdce7f02cdfa78881c7e355c9aada4134cf06b663a2deefb3d779b9ca.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=8x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =8x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =8\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/04/0475e2e272a30318dc4cb31457539a312544b6e14d7e6a8ed3f911d41404b575.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186511547 :question/id #uuid "b6ef3a51-3ce7-571a-8d2a-d26c504b1810" :question/math-academy-id "q-161923" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1619dc0b-d53c-58c4-92e8-5b68a431da0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510831} {:answer/id #uuid "35312181-3164-564e-951d-368b81aed2bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510899} {:answer/id #uuid "4c7493ae-3582-5f1c-82f8-0c2dae976bc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-3\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510948} {:answer/id #uuid "90ead743-a1fc-5f4f-9075-c4fd3b6866f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186511080} {:answer/id #uuid "c72bf197-8bb8-5cea-9e15-63920f550d30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186511195}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186510831} :answer-field/id #uuid "60daa8fe-705e-5990-9f0d-a1092f6eb497" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186511360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/98/989c9452bebc4ee6c2253c920655830a0b3d0adf0ddb7b90c1ea6a9528ef1448.png)

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$  represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(-3,0,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-6x$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-6x \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-6\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](images/df/df8a9da3b88f3b40d85005b156215f7fa7760257f284acf98ec186d5a2e3ab8d.png)

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$

$$

$$
{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin.

![](images/6f/6f35be4fd6773149597ea8a9dc8dd234e068da3f0fd3b2df32d11c61521bed75.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{2},\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186374027 :question/id #uuid "79d3cb68-3e16-5f1e-b189-33638dfa47d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-161760" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129281 :knowledge-point/id #uuid $$

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin.

![](images/8c/8c803dbf5bcf6c2ece6c1c8352f96da1c88734ca1d792dd05593ac8c11527b2b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

$$

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](images/d2/d2b9c6f3541c47f37ad7f2ba52d739787e39600ec71fe3530f0ad2846c24880b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186511483 :question/id #uuid "3eee5be8-fdde-5369-b6f0-771204d5bd54" :question/math-academy-id "q-161775" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1888a529-95b0-58f6-9146-6b50fc190c6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510838} {:answer/id #uuid "3756a535-be12-51cb-a4f4-eebb7d355566" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510908} {:answer/id #uuid "557a8050-44a3-59e1-8a70-aa6bd1dd5460" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510964} {:answer/id #uuid "5b788302-0dfd-54bf-a49b-6d49283dd409" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186510974} {:answer/id #uuid "c886c152-17ed-511e-a809-d63c2213db33" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ" :db/id 17592186511198}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186510964} :answer-field/id #uuid "024d0b3c-4d66-50af-a789-68c23cbe417a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186511309}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ for $y\le 0$ and $z\ge 0.$

[{:db/id 17592186130203 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

For example, suppose we want to evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown below.

![](images/08/0809a74f0aca2b3042b7f8db6783f9d6a13bc84bfc75ddcbb4d3076dbf0a2efd.png)

This integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because

- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and

- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined by

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

The preimage of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)

To express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

It can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2\sin\phi.
$$

Therefore, the change of variables formula is

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

Now, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\  & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{\rho }^{6}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b86207dc-5c0f-5e73-a894-7cd428b18036" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0355ca44-2058-5e43-b562-1ba67c747a89" :step/math-academy-id 44584 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130205}} {:db/id 17592186130235 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi,
$$

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}|-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot (-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ))-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86bd6cae-b4e6-5da9-80b3-b884c320bda3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7720 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Jacobian for Spherical Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "96fb4483-0ca7-52c1-9f83-46c894da5471" :step/math-academy-id 44767 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130236}} {:db/id 17592186130236 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130469 :tutorial/content "We can also derive the change of variables formula for spherical polar coordinates using geometry.

Consider a bounded spherical box $R,$ given by

$$
R = \big\{ (\rho,\theta,\phi) \: | \: a \leq \rho \leq b, \:\: \alpha \leq \theta \leq \beta, \:\: \gamma \leq \phi \leq \psi \big\}.
$$

We can divide each interval into $l,m,$ and $n$ subdivisions such that 

$$
\Delta\rho = \dfrac{b-a}{l},\qquad \Delta\theta = \dfrac{\beta-\alpha}{m},\qquad \Delta\phi = \dfrac{\psi-\gamma}{n}.
$$

This splits the region into "spherical wedges," as shown in the following diagram.

![](images/88/88be4c6a09062321d20ac7f48dfbb6be796cdd6b5bb1b7f6adc49a6ae1da609b.png)

Zooming in on one of these wedges, we obtain a shape resembling a rectangular solid.

![](images/5e/5e5f7acb4d057e856c66e9d5626f81178ca26c0b7ce83cdf7290b1f4c64b1852.png)

Let's note the volume of this solid as $\Delta V.$ To approximate the value of $\Delta V,$ we use the formula for the volume of a rectangular solid:

$$
\Delta V \approx lwh
$$

Clearly, the height of the rectangular solid is $h = \Delta \rho.$ We can find the remaining dimensions using simple geometry. 

First, we need to find the length of the radius $r$ in the $xy$-plane. Using the following triangle and a side-on view of the wedge, we conclude that $r=\rho\sin\phi.$

![](images/01/0122c6c3b813bbe2821dbede794b6027cd69002dd1828925811211045a0d67e8.png)

Let's add this to our diagram.

![](images/d4/d41b538e9bb3add9bae1e3a24c9f87ae282a8b969f0c0dc4acd374ad777de74a.png)

Finally, we can use the arc length formula $s = r \cdot \theta$ to find the length $l$ and width $w.$

![](images/88/882b9243d1189c098aaf6e1e45ca7ec97d480b1f2c3a8fe23d5e39a6c2313ed2.png)

The length of our wedge is 

$$
l = \rho \cdot \Delta\phi = \rho\Delta\phi
$$

 and the width is 

$$
w = \rho\sin\phi \cdot \Delta\theta = \rho\sin\phi\Delta\theta.
$$

Calculating the volume as a rectangular solid, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}ΔV & ≈lwh \\  & =(\rho Δϕ)\cdot (\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕΔ\theta )\cdot (Δ\rho ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,Δϕ\,Δ\theta \,Δ\rho .\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we define the triple integral in spherical coordinates as the limit of a triple Riemann sum, where $(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk})$ being any sample point in the spherical subregion $B{ijk}{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{l,m,n \to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{l} \sum\limits_{j=1}^{m} \sum\limits_{k=1}^{n} f(\rho_{ijk},\theta_{ijk},\phi_{ijk}) (\rho_{ijk})^2 \sin \phi_{ijk} \:\Delta\rho\:\Delta\theta\:\Delta\phi
$$

As we increase the number of subregions, the size of $\Delta\rho,$ $\Delta\theta,$ and $\Delta\phi$ all goes to zero, and the volume of $R$ is more accurately approximated, giving

$$
\textrm{d}V = \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that if $f(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ is continuous on a spherical box $R = [a,b] \times [\alpha,\beta] \times [\gamma, \psi],$ then

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \:\textrm{d}V
=
\iiint\limits_{R} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi
=
\int_{\gamma}^{\psi}\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\int_{a}^{b} f(\rho,\theta,\phi) \rho^2 \sin\phi \:\textrm{d}\rho\:\textrm{d}\theta\:\textrm{d}\phi.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "444d88e7-62f3-5333-98ad-9ee9e22d6a46" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7730 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Change of Variables Formula Using Geometry"} :step/id #uuid "68b6f2fa-a8c8-5b52-98b8-fd02b1454611" :step/math-academy-id 44789}] :activity/title "Triple Integrals in Spherical Polar Coordinates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129390} {:db/id 17592186130203 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

This integral seems too challenging when written in Cartesian coordinates. However, we should recognize that the problem lends itself to spherical polar coordinates because

- the domain $R$ has a simple spherical polar representation, and

- the integrand $f(x,y,z)=\left(x^2+y^2+z^2\right)^{3/2}$ can also be expressed simply in spherical polar coordinates.

So, let's transform the entire problem to spherical polar coordinates using the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ defined by

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi.
$$

The preimage of $R$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/c2/c2ed8a57c5e66687428a524eb148f96672f3a1ace7fbd28d426de065b2fb5f1f.png)

To express our integral in terms of spherical polar coordinates, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

It can be shown that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant for a spherical change of variables is

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2\sin\phi.
$$

Therefore, the change of variables formula is

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

Now, let's write our function $f(x,y,z) = \left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2\right)^{3/2}$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & ={({\rho }^{2})}^{3/2} \\  & ={\rho }^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}^{3/2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{3}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{\rho }^{5}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{6}{\rho }^{6}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot \frac{1}{6}(1-0) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b86207dc-5c0f-5e73-a894-7cd428b18036" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7149 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0355ca44-2058-5e43-b562-1ba67c747a89" :step/math-academy-id 42751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130204}} {:db/id 17592186130455 :tutorial/content "When evaluating triple integrals, it's sometimes easier to change the variables from Cartesian coordinates to spherical polar coordinates.

:tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi,
$$

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & 0 & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}|-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & -\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot (-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ))-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{cos}^{2}⁡ϕ-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡ϕ+{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =-{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "86bd6cae-b4e6-5da9-80b3-b884c320bda3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7720 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Jacobian for Spherical Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "96fb4483-0ca7-52c1-9f83-46c894da5471" :step/math-academy-id 44767 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130236}} {:db/id 17592186130468 :tutorial/content "Throughout this lesson, we've used the fact that 

$$
\left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (\rho, \theta, \phi)} \right| = \rho^2 \sin{\phi}.
$$

Let's now prove this result.

Given the spherical coordinate transformations

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

we first  calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂\theta } & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂x}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂y}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta } & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂y}{∂ϕ} & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \frac{∂z}{∂\rho } & =\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ & \,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta } & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂ϕ} & =-\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
