Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/f3/f393d0facc98fe365e2c622e24223d6045b48b490937ba6e2f25d86d7eb4810f.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-8{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459266 :question/id #uuid "a7d3359f-1209-53f1-b438-cca94d3b404c" :question/math-academy-id "q-126737" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186176023 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b2eca638-7c7b-51ed-99e3-3b3156d13669" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Line Integral Using Green's Theorem"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24f7045b-5228-59f7-a899-69db8a29caed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186458702} {:answer/id #uuid "64eeeb99-1d14-5f8d-8274-71cc4b59f7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458803} {:answer/id #uuid "8f089fd7-57f0-5309-8b86-329b4b579d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186458877} {:answer/id #uuid "b143a56b-f222-5495-aa7a-9092c0670a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186458946} {:answer/id #uuid "bbe1ae9b-b60a-5838-a56d-dad4b77ce8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186458967}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "bbe1ae9b-b60a-5838-a56d-dad4b77ce8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186458967} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3e4c3bc-9dab-52ff-8019-5399ade463a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186459196}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/fb/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"}] :question/problem "Given that
![](images/1e/1e78bf74df5607a1d80b3bd51b3222505e3bb201817448a7a5ebe5b0a73cffa9.svg)
where $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle y^2+\sin x, \: 3xy-\cos y  \right\rangle$ and $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (y^2+\sin x) \: \mathrm{d}x + (3xy-\cos y) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/79/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)= y^2+\sin x$ and $Q(x,y)= 3xy-\cos y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx+(xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0\leq r \leq 2,\: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi  \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $r^2\sin\theta.$"} {:db/id 17592186051070} {:db/id 17592186176311 :question/id #uuid "e77d34a7-9f25-5206-895c-5f4fa0d1f689" :question/math-academy-id "q-125716"} {:db/id where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$

$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/b9/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186459234 :question/id #uuid "48fe30a0-5320-52ad-9ed5-45000abef204" :question/math-academy-id "q-126532" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f21bd52-4aa7-5ea8-a034-d3560d1d5b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458686} {:answer/id #uuid "648aec14-e325-59f4-a6ad-4fe7fed0f4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186458801} {:answer/id #uuid "6c53cfdb-2fdd-546b-ab1b-dc3144c77b6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458818} {:answer/id #uuid "76be6580-ecd9-54fd-be34-2e6d6eb3bf26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458837} {:answer/id #uuid "867e3063-71a8-5b3f-ba08-0e4184738773" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-1" :db/id 17592186458863}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458818} :answer-field/id #uuid "7bb86058-0e7f-5528-b79d-a77b82e246b7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/04/0470588a034222b183694b087d417e8ead0d2fd72357e796373794d00523708f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186537903 :question/id #uuid "37e413b5-1ec6-5915-aa78-dfcf790b6b22" :question/math-academy-id "q-126519"} {:db/id 17592186537955 :question/id #uuid "Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0b5a23c7-4ccf-5122-8b5f-98fbabb0e367" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5838 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0b3de726-ead0-5369-a1fe-3dcc61b38bbc" :step/math-academy-id 35776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176808}} {:db/id 17592186176808 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186051070}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176311} {:db/id 17592186176485} {:db/id 17592186262625} {:db/id 17592186262628} {:db/id 17592186262632} {:db/id 17592186405036} {:db/id 17592186405043} {:db/id 17592186416111} {:db/id 17592186459234} {:db/id 17592186537903} {:db/id 17592186537955}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "f69ccccf-5d34-5f08-95d0-7af5d0c7628b" :step/math-academy-id 35777 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176735}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Polar Coordinates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176145} {:db/id 17592186176807 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177037 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

:question/problem "![](images/eb/eb2da6fbb22b19d027212685ca521f5186a831502617c2089766c5e9fe739696.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy\,?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/48/4822bfa926feccb0a12c14580ac325f4f10a0e4f815d0247b2231bf08b8c2326.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x+3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x))\,dx+({x}^{2}+3xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "33aa2c01-ef8c-530d-9a87-558d09200d7c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459337}} {:db/id 17592186459332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459223 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "76e9497e-95ac-551f-b7f9-a976c2b420b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458839} {:answer/id #uuid "8daee35f-46c8-5466-b3b4-c225766c4214" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\pi " :db/id 17592186458874} {:answer/id #uuid "9f77bfdf-543d-55d9-98f8-52a2f2343148" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\pi " :db/id 17592186458910} {:answer/id #uuid "a61402b4-43f9-5d6a-b293-8db1d57747f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\pi " :db/id 17592186458925} {:answer/id #uuid "e782fbf2-3eee-5d13-a745-b3e38c6a490e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186459031}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458910} :answer-field/id #uuid "16ca1c58-b325-53c7-b363-8ad3f071412f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459095}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3227ab6b-7873-5e0c-8df6-f96bbac69dd6" :question/math-academy-id "q-126735" :question/problem "![](images/1f/1f56006dd06fab3bbc736c45ac6e9d65a401b88e0a9eb8a5db404fb67b89977e.png)

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/f3/f393d0facc98fe365e2c622e24223d6045b48b490937ba6e2f25d86d7eb4810f.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-8{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=8{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-8{x}^{2}y)dx+({y}^{7}+8x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(8{y}^{2}-(-8{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}8({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}8{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}[2{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}32\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32[\theta ]_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =32\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =16\pi .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b39e3053-19ff-54d9-8a03-cabe47ece267" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459334}} {:db/id 17592186459334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459266 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24f7045b-5228-59f7-a899-69db8a29caed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186458702} {:answer/id #uuid "64eeeb99-1d14-5f8d-8274-71cc4b59f7db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\pi " :db/id 17592186458803} {:answer/id #uuid "8f089fd7-57f0-5309-8b86-329b4b579d58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186458877} {:answer/id #uuid "b143a56b-f222-5495-aa7a-9092c0670a7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186458946} {:answer/id #uuid "bbe1ae9b-b60a-5838-a56d-dad4b77ce8e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186458967}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458967} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3e4c3bc-9dab-52ff-8019-5399ade463a4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459196}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a7d3359f-1209-53f1-b438-cca94d3b404c" :question/math-academy-id "q-126737" :question/problem "![](images/fb/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb7edd78-bd6a-5d85-baab-eeb17426674d"} {:db/id 17592186459335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459234 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f21bd52-4aa7-5ea8-a034-d3560d1d5b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458686} {:answer/id #uuid "648aec14-e325-59f4-a6ad-4fe7fed0f4d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta " :db/id 17592186458801} {:answer/id #uuid "6c53cfdb-2fdd-546b-ab1b-dc3144c77b6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458818} {:answer/id #uuid "76be6580-ecd9-54fd-be34-2e6d6eb3bf26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r" :db/id 17592186458837} {:answer/id #uuid "867e3063-71a8-5b3f-ba08-0e4184738773" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-1" :db/id 17592186458863}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458818} :answer-field/id #uuid "7bb86058-0e7f-5528-b79d-a77b82e246b7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "48fe30a0-5320-52ad-9ed5-45000abef204" :question/math-academy-id "q-126532" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/04/0470588a034222b183694b087d417e8ead0d2fd72357e796373794d00523708f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d286d5c7-a12c-594f-9ccb-48543ab9d3ae" :step/next {:db/id 17592186459319}} {:db/id 17592186459337 :step/content {:db/id 17592186459263 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14eb9fcd-7abf-50ea-acb9-8e896cb286b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458663} {:answer/id #uuid "4752d255-6d05-5b8c-9bc7-d3d564d74fbb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458759} {:answer/id #uuid "4d3491ea-d8ce-5605-97f6-fd42cbc08809" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458767} {:answer/id #uuid "62d8034f-3c24-592c-b26b-73464d3851ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}({r}^{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458798} {:answer/id #uuid "778250fc-a408-537b-8277-d49912ff9021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta " :db/id 17592186458840}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186458767} :answer-field/id #uuid "294a80e3-eaa7-5f33-b4a3-69d8d31c5ae7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186459103}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a150df94-0dd2-516e-ab2f-283c22ad4f30" :question/math-academy-id "q-126707" :question/problem "![](images/18/184b50ce54b01453d5b645eef7edc186823e8ae34afaefa2527e34122c1722cc.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/93/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}

$$

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

$$

$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/93/93a1c20377ddd0731c6190712d9d6d77551124fa33001334e84f52049bb6b800.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1+2{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,dx+(\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+10)+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-(1+2{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 9,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{9}(1-2{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above." :question/worked-solution "Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/d8/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cb7edd78-bd6a-5d85-baab-eeb17426674d"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f21bd52-4aa7-5ea8-a034-d3560d1d5b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$
V = lwh
$$

$$

$$

$$

One-third of the carton is filled with juice, forming a cube. Find the volume of the empty space in the carton.

![](images/90/90280dd78d285df5dc798c3ec90b7fb47a72414f2934d36885eb9d65fd7584fd.png)" :question/worked-solution "The orange juice in the carton creates a cube. Since the height of the juice is $9\,\textrm{cm}$, the side length of the cube is also $9\,\textrm{cm}$.

The height of $9 \: \textrm{cm}$ shown in the diagram represents a third of the carton's height. Therefore, the height of the carton is

$$
3 \cdot 9 = 27 \: \textrm{cm}
$$

The empty space in the carton is a rectangular prism that is $9\:\textrm{cm}$ long, $9\:\textrm{cm}$ wide, and

$$
27 - 9 = 18\:\textrm{cm}
$$

high.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V = lwh
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting

$$
l=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad w=9\,\textrm{cm}, \qquad h=18\,\textrm{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V = 9 \cdot 9 \cdot 18 = 1\,458\:\textrm{cm}^3
$$

Therefore, we conclude that there is $1\,458 \: \textrm{cm}^3$ of empty space in the carton."} {:db/id 17592186120088 :question/id #uuid "f9fb6d92-70dd-5c7f-9979-070fe590bd5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-107738" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119892 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ba5bf1d9-f6e2-5494-91fd-31c20d7fa09b" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Volume of a Rectangular Solid: Word Problems"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "94e026db-b6ca-5d1f-bc3c-3be6b14dd14a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$$1.80$" :db/id 17592186116735} {:answer/id #uuid "aaf356cf-15b6-5092-9788-e98b4f596935" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$$8.50$" :db/id 17592186116736} {:answer/id #uuid "d22f8719-b0f3-5d7a-8f03-f8cb18846173" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$$7.20$" :db/id 17592186116737} {:answer/id #uuid "f581f57c-328a-511b-adf3-7882b27f3560" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$$7.02$" :db/id 17592186116738} {:answer/id #uuid "35dc34cf-6ed5-588b-8665-51cdf9e08eda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "$$6.20$" :db/id 17592186116739}] :answer-field/id #uuid "8e3ac18f-df2a-531e-80f1-3bbd339896a0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186116734}] :question/problem "A bar of chocolate in the form of a rectangular prism is $9cm$ long, $5cm$ wide, and $2cm$ high. "2737d1a7-2af9-54ed-8c42-5191fc68a31b" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Volume of a Solid Using the Shell Method"}] :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=3y-y^2$ and $x=y$, as shown below. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.

![](images/7e/7eca2a7eecfb9555a7e1555555a6d7b435a794e5715537d4fe94998ef00d124a.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let

$$
f(y)=3y-y^2
$$

and $g(y)=y$.

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(y) &= g(y) \\
3y - y^{2} &= y \\
2y - y^{2} &= 0 \\
y(2 - y) &= 0 \\
y &= 0, 2
\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions corresponding to our region are $y=0$ and $y=2$. So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=2$.

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/86/861a1300845e3832a201dd00410d462350f33a4654332b6b6fa7140dc6476dbb.png)

The horizontal arrow

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=y$, and
- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=3y-y^2$.

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= 2π\int_{c}^{d}y([right] - [left])dy \\
&= 2π\int_{0}^{2}y([3y - y^{2}] - [y])dy \\
&= 2π\int_{0}^{2}y(2y - y^{2})dy \\
&= 2π\int_{0}^{2}(2y^{2} - y^{3})dy \\
&= 2π(2\int_{0}^{2}y^{2}dy - \int_{0}^{2}y^{3}dy) \\
&= 2π(2 \cdot \left.\frac{y^{3}}{3}\right|_{0}^{2} - \left.\frac{y^{4}}{4}\right|_{0}^{2}) \\
&= 2π(2(\frac{8}{3} - 0) - (\frac{16}{4} - 0)) \\
&= 2π(\frac{16}{3} - 4) \\
&= \frac{8π}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176404 :question/id #uuid "36b6fba6-7714-5e86-b561-3885022f2455" :question/math-academy-id "q-17029"} {:db/id 17592186176406 :question/id #uuid "cb3b2ae0-3684-5588-a899-0fbf11d8930b" :question/math-academy-id "q-17032"} {:db/id 17592186175969 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175819 :question/id #uuid "9f7f3606-5c49-51d0-b4e5-cffd0310b6c1" :question/math-academy-id "e-8857"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3cd62b9c-0fbc-5a1e-b923-b2be8a55e44a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176215 :question/id #uuid "63dab448-9512-5530-9d1b-9f6d7896aa95" :question/math-academy-id "q-107098"} {:db/id 17592186176403 :question/id #uuid "2289657c-a9c3-56eb-97a8-f3d9729a0b73" :question/math-academy-id "q-17023"}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"} {:db/id 17592186175819 :question/id #uuid "9f7f3606-5c49-51d0-b4e5-cffd0310b6c1" :question/math-academy-id "e-8857" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186175969 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3cd62b9c-0fbc-5a1e-b923-b2be8a55e44a" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"}] :question/problem "Consider the finite region bounded by the curves $x=2-y^2$, $x=y$, and the $x$-axis, as shown below. Using the shell method, find an integral expression for the volume generated when this region is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.

![](images/fa/fa2a775faed9c425a3b94e417b761d11486b4f41dae3129d9c9e016c28a652f0.png)" :question/worked-solution "First, let

$$
f(y)=2-y^2
$$

and $g(y)=y$.

We start by determining the points where the curves intersect by solving the following equation for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(y) &= g(y) \\
2 - y^{2} &= y \\
y^{2} + y - 2 &= 0 \\
(y + 2)(y - 1) &= 0 \\
y &= -2, 1
\end{aligned}
$$

The solution corresponding to our region is $y=1$. So, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1$.

Now, let's draw our usual horizontal arrow through the region to determine the left and right functions.

![](images/4c/4cc38a21168a86d2b64289e9c7877fbff4bf976b7214ed4befeb9644894f6172.png)

The horizontal arrow

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=g(y)=y$, and
- *leaves* through the right function $x=f(y)=2-y^2$.

Therefore, using the shell method, the volume of the solid can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V &= 2π\int_{c}^{d}y([right] - [left])dy \\
&= 2π\int_{0}^{1}y([2 - y^{2}] - [y])dy \\
&= 2π\int_{0}^{1}y(2 - y - y^{2})dy
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186176215 :question/id #uuid "63dab448-9512-5530-9d1b-9f6d7896aa95" :question/math-academy-id "q-107098"} {:db/id 17592186176403 :question/id #uuid "2289657c-a9c3-56eb-97a8-f3d9729a0b73" :question/math-academy-id "q-17023" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186175969 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3cd62b9c-0fbc-5a1e-b923-b2be8a55e44a" :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ba2acd00-9b53-53b6-ab77-4f405beaee41" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}y(4y - 2y^{2})dy" :db/id 17592186174677} {:answer/id #uuid "d71365f0-76a4-5135-8feb-bb4b94aaac69" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}y(2y^{2} - 4y)^{2}dy" :db/id 17592186174678} {:answer/id #uuid "d8db48f2-8530-5ffc-b6fe-aa0cd877d5bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}y(6y - 2y^{2})dy" :db/id 17592186174679} {:answer/id #uuid "da491968-8279-58a2-8f9e-4f73a8cbab30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}y(2y^{2} - 4y)dy" :db/id 17592186174680} {:answer/id #uuid "36e48c5d-45b8-5f5e-8a05-a5164f6ff937" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2π\displaystyle \int_{0}^{2}(4y - 2y^{2})^{2}dy" :db/id 17592186174681}] :answer-field/id #uuid "ab089e7c-7f52-5582-ac6f-752c4f8bf60f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186174676}] :question/problem "![](images/a5/a5a3a246f2ecb4bee6cfc46f34d14b5abc9fcf22ed0d6173ed465bfab2cfeca6.png)

:topic/id #uuid "4d4dd9cc-d32a-5514-bbc8-b9d4357f3376" :topic/math-academy-id 6007} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186209870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209878 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar functions to include quadratic functions, quadratic forms, and the chain rule.

Consider the (scalar) **quadratic function**

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a matrix, and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n$ is a column vector. We wish to calculate the gradient of this function:

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf x} f = \nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}\right)
$$

We start by showing that $f$ can be written in the expanded form 

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

To understand why this is the same as $\mathbf x^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf x,$ let's first write
![](images/39/394b4241f76616fae493bcc281cbe782c1d1a89680ef24cd2776c02302b9550d.svg)

Now, we compute $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$ by working step by step.

First, we compute the product $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$, which gives us an $n\times 1$ column vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & ⋯ & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & ⋯ & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1} & {a}_{n2} & ⋯ & {a}_{nn}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}{x}_{1}+{a}_{12}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{1n}{x}_{n} \\ {a}_{21}{x}_{1}+{a}_{22}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{2n}{x}_{n} \\ ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1}{x}_{1}+{a}_{n2}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{nn}{x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{1j}{x}_{j} \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{2j}{x}_{j} \\ ⋮ \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{nj}{x}_{j}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply $\mathbf{x}^T$ by this result:
![](images/15/15180b9898708fa3f2398a534c0e4f0a57f4466abd046b388eb7af3009e534b0.svg)

Each term of this product looks like $x_i \cdot \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j$, so the full expression becomes

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j \right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

So, we've shown that

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.}
$$

Let's now discuss how this helps us to compute the gradient of $f.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46d7287c-3842-57d9-8f8b-8f5f95c5362f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12386 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b43433a0-9dff-53f0-b8cf-64336b4b2fc7" :step/math-academy-id 610963 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209871}} {:db/id 17592186209871 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209954 :tutorial/content "We have the quadratic function

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}
$$

where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a matrix, and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n$ is a column vector. As we've seen, $f$ can be written in the expanded form

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

We'll use this form to compute the gradient of $f.$

To compute the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f$, we'll differentiate this expanded form with respect to $x_k.$ First, we express our expanded function as

$$
f(\mathbf x) =  \sum_{i \neq k} \sum_{j \neq k} A_{ij} x_i x_j 
+ \sum_{i \neq k} A_{ik} x_i x_k 
+ \sum_{j \neq k} A_{kj} x_k x_j 
+ A_{kk} x_k^2.
$$

The idea here is to break up the double summation by isolating all the terms that involve the variable $x_k$. 

Notice that

- the first summation is *independent* of $x_k,$

- the second and third summations are *linear* in $x_k,$ and

- the final term is *quadratic* in $x_k.$

We can now compute our derivative term by term in a structured way. Differentiating with respect to $x_k,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{k}} & =\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{k}}[{\sum }_{i\ne k}{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{ij}{x}_{i}{x}_{j}+{\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}{x}_{k}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{k}{x}_{j}+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}^{2}] \\  & ={\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j}+2{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & =({\sum }_{i\ne k}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k}+({\sum }_{j\ne k}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j})+{A}_{kk}{x}_{k} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{A}_{ik}{x}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{A}_{kj}{x}_{j} \\  & =({A}^{T}x)_{k}+(Ax)_{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is true for all $1\leq k \leq n$, we get the result

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = A^T \mathbf{x} + A \mathbf{x} = (A^T + A)\mathbf x.
$$

From here, we have the following special cases:

- If $A$ is symmetric, then $A^T = A,$ $f(\mathbf x)$ is a quadratic form, and our result simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}) = 2 A \mathbf{x}.
$$

- Suppose that $A = I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. Then, our result for symmetric matrices simplifies to

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} (\mathbf{x}^T  \mathbf{x}) = 2 \mathbf{x}
$$

which is a result we saw in a previous lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "332e4bab-6a1d-5868-a616-4a2c034c2619" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13115 :tutorial/title "The Gradient of a Quadratic Function"} :step/id #uuid "b7685ad5-7aa7-532e-936b-bd0ad89e40bd" :step/math-academy-id 610964 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209872}} {:db/id 17592186209872 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208846 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208271 :question/id #uuid "a06524d0-6980-52eb-b5fb-2ca7d0c1dbac" :question/math-academy-id "e-17350"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9fe0d364-ef22-5138-9ee5-e473bd909447" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048851} {:db/id 17592186049450}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186208924} {:db/id 17592186208925} {:db/id 17592186532650} {:db/id 17592186532661} {:db/id 17592186532671} {:db/id 17592186532724}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Form"} :step/id #uuid "1f3213b1-5ea3-5cd6-9b86-84bd1ef095b3" :step/math-academy-id 610965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209873}} {:db/id 17592186209873 :step/content {:db/id 17592186208847 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186208289 :question/id #uuid "b4e84c40-15d1-585f-84c7-c615979cd8f5" :question/math-academy-id "e-18713"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2198cf08-3a99-5e5d-80af-bbe722b51647" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186208956} {:db/id 17592186208957} {:db/id 17592186532652} {:db/id 17592186532660} {:db/id 17592186532689} {:db/id 17592186532692}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing Gradient of a Quadratic Function"} :step/id #uuid "bc662f29-b540-527e-bb28-752fc9820d44" :step/math-academy-id 610968 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209874}} {:db/id 17592186209874 :step/content {:db/id 17592186209877 :tutorial/content "Now, let $\mathbf{y}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^q$ and $f: \mathbb{R}^q \to \mathbb{R}$. Suppose we want to compute the gradient 

$$

To do this, we need to apply the chain rule. The chain rule for total derivatives tells us that

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{1 \times n}
=

\cdot 
\underbrace{\frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}}_{q \times n}.

$$
\underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
$$

To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={{{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{n\times q}\cdot {{{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient chain rule is

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
\cdot 
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f.
$$

Consider the (scalar) **quadratic function**

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a matrix, and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n$ is a column vector. We wish to calculate the gradient of this function:

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf x} f = \nabla_{\mathbf x} \left(\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}\right)
$$

We start by showing that $f$ can be written in the expanded form 

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

To understand why this is the same as $\mathbf x^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf x,$ let's first write
![](images/39/394b4241f76616fae493bcc281cbe782c1d1a89680ef24cd2776c02302b9550d.svg)

Now, we compute $\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$ by working step by step.

First, we compute the product $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}$, which gives us an $n\times 1$ column vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & ⋯ & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & ⋯ & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1} & {a}_{n2} & ⋯ & {a}_{nn}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}{x}_{1}+{a}_{12}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{1n}{x}_{n} \\ {a}_{21}{x}_{1}+{a}_{22}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{2n}{x}_{n} \\ ⋮ \\ {a}_{n1}{x}_{1}+{a}_{n2}{x}_{2}+⋯+{a}_{nn}{x}_{n}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{1j}{x}_{j} \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{2j}{x}_{j} \\ ⋮ \\ {\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{nj}{x}_{j}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply $\mathbf{x}^T$ by this result:
![](images/15/15180b9898708fa3f2398a534c0e4f0a57f4466abd046b388eb7af3009e534b0.svg)

Each term of this product looks like $x_i \cdot \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j$, so the full expression becomes

$$
\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \left( \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_j \right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.
$$

So, we've shown that

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} x_i x_j.}
$$

Let's now discuss how this helps us to compute the gradient of $f.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "46d7287c-3842-57d9-8f8b-8f5f95c5362f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12386 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b43433a0-9dff-53f0-b8cf-64336b4b2fc7" :step/math-academy-id 610963 :step/next {:db/id 17592186209871}} {:db/id 17592186209878 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll extend our knowledge of gradients of scalar functions to include quadratic functions, quadratic forms, and the chain rule.

\underbrace{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f}_{n \times 1} = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} f}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
$$

To derive the chain rule in terms of gradients, we apply the identity $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & ={{{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{n\times q}\cdot {{{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y})}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{q\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the gradient chain rule is

$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} f = 
\left( \frac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{y}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}} \right)^T
\cdot 
\nabla_{\mathbf{y}} f.
$$

Note that the order matters; when expressed in the gradient form, the derivatives are applied *from right to left!*" :tutorial/id #uuid "eb90df7d-906c-5d50-a61a-40222511f26e" :tutorial/math-academy-id [{:db/id 17592186101763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101920 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have an alternating series

$$
S = \sum_{n =1}^\infty b_n
$$

where

$$
b_n = (-1)^n a_n
$$

or

$$
b_n = (-1)^{n+1} a_n
$$

with

$$
a_n \geq 0
$$

Let's assume that the above series is convergent by the alternating series test.

The $N$th partial sum of this series is

$$
s_n = \sum_{n =1}^N b_n
$$

How good an estimate of $S$ is the $n$th partial sum of $S$?

The **alternating series error bound** states that, for a convergent alternating series,

$$
\begin{vmatrix}S- s_n & < & b_{n+1}\end{vmatrix}
$$

In other words, the magnitude of the error of the $n$th partial sum is less than the magnitude of the $(n+1)$th term." :tutorial/id #uuid "d1ab9f29-4499-5933-a4db-cf6fd5292dd6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1260 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cc3fd837-dffb-53ad-8a81-f754a99bdf38" :step/math-academy-id 2473 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101764}} {:db/id 17592186101764 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100924 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100772 :question/id #uuid "dfa7cfd6-08dd-507f-aa3a-61beacbc36ca" :question/math-academy-id "e-721"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c1ad1fe5-c690-54ab-a172-fdc69668d60d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050417}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101191} {:db/id 17592186101467} {:db/id 17592186536809}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Alternating Series Error Bound for a Given Partial Sum"} :step/id #uuid "a6217776-80ac-51aa-9ea0-f5fce39fdb15" :step/math-academy-id 2474 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101765}} {:db/id 17592186101765 :step/content {:db/id 17592186100925 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100774 :question/id #uuid "193d6ccc-ffa5-5f36-8ed1-084dea29448f" :question/math-academy-id "e-723"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "be83d82e-531e-52bf-bacb-b621694ce40c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101186} {:db/id 17592186101464}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Values of N Such That the Error in the Nth Partial Sum Is Smaller Than a Given Number"} :step/id #uuid "05d18ce2-c320-5098-8bb6-ce9ee0b599e9" :step/math-academy-id 2480}] :activity/title "The Alternating Series Error Bound" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186101041} {:db/id 17592186101763 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101920 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have an alternating series

:question/problem "Express $\log_3(2)+\log_3(5)$ as a single logarithm." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{3} 2 + \log_{3} 5 &= \log_{3} (2 \cdot 5) \\
&= \log_{3} 10

"First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
3\log_{5} 7 + 3\log_{5} 3 &= 3(\log_{5} 7 + \log_{5} 3) \\
&= 3\log_{5} (7 \cdot 3) \\
&= 3\log_{5} 21
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
3\log_{5}{7}+3\log_{5}{3} = 3\log_{5} 21
$$"} {:db/id 17592186111033 :question/id #uuid "76b19b94-8e77-533e-8352-d0260491a779" :question/math-academy-id "q-24434"} {:db/id 17592186111067 :question/id #uuid "66cada22-da7f-54d5-8420-b271c437409b" :question/math-academy-id "q-25925"} {:db/id 17592186110698 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110488 :question/id #uuid "679a8e3b-ef6c-565d-ab37-613dedfdf3df" :question/math-academy-id "e-4016"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d65ce7f4-c4c9-5620-bc55-01017d98272f" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111210 :question/id #uuid "6b207bb1-fb19-5946-bdc6-deed023b9159" :question/math-academy-id "q-47209"} {:db/id 17592186111211 :question/id #uuid "c1d0421d-ffc1-5952-bf2a-e2642960f555" :question/math-academy-id "q-47210"}] :knowledge-point/title "Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule"} {:db/id 17592186110488 :question/id #uuid "679a8e3b-ef6c-565d-ab37-613dedfdf3df" :question/math-academy-id "e-4016" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186110698 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d65ce7f4-c4c9-5620-bc55-01017d98272f" :knowledge-point/title "Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule"}] :question/problem "Express $\ln\left(x^2 y\right)$ as a sum of two logarithms." :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the product rule for natural logarithms:

$$

$$

$$

\ln (x^{2}y) &= \ln (x^{2} \cdot y) \\
&= \ln (x^{2}) + \ln y
\end{aligned}

The **product rule** states that two logarithms which share a common base $\color{blue}n$ satisfy

$$
\log_{\color{blue}n}(a) + \log_{\color{blue}n}(b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left(ab\right)
$$

So, we can use the product rule to rewrite $\log_{\color{blue}5}(4) + \log_{\color{blue}5}(3)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_{5} 4 + \log_{5} (3) &= \log_{5} (4 \cdot 3) \\
&= \log_{5} (12)
\end{aligned}
$$

The product rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms." :tutorial/id #uuid "a915130a-f6b9-5fec-a625-3d6d987255ac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2782 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} For example, suppose that a store sells two packs of shirts:

- $3$ shirts for $\[math]12$

- $5$ shirts for $\[/math]15$

To determine which pack is the better deal, we can compare their unit prices.

- For the pack of $3$ shirts for $\[math]12,$ dividing the total cost by the total number of shirts gives

$$
12 \div 3 = 4.
$$

So, the unit price is $\[/math]4.$

- For the pack of $5$ shirts for $\[math]15,$ dividing the total cost by the total number of shirts gives

$$
15 \div 5 = 3.
$$

So, the unit price is $\[/math]3.$

Now we interpret the unit prices in the context of the problem.

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}

We know that the derivative of the hyperbolic sine is the hyperbolic cosine:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sinh{x}) = \cosh{x}
$$

Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we have

$$
\int \cosh{x}\,\textrm d x = \sinh{x} + C.
$$

Similarly, by considering the derivative of the hyperbolic cosine, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\cosh x) = \sinh{x} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \int \sinh x\  \textrm{d}x = \cosh x + C.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d780519f-20fa-5840-be56-4a5f0539ed6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5211 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1f4742a6-369c-57f0-9437-c9e83653cf97" :step/math-academy-id 32696 :step/next {:db/id 17592186065183}} {:db/id 17592186065188 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065392 :tutorial/content "$\newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}

:question/worked-solution "The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

is given by

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We substitute $a=2$ and $b=-12$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= - ((-12))/(2(2)) \\
&= - ((-12))/(4) \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=3$."} {:db/id 17592186049919} {:db/id 17592186083620 :question/id #uuid "666db282-5f92-5a61-a462-84aa546c0cc4" :question/math-academy-id "q-220351"} {:db/id 17592186083655 :question/id #uuid "97de26b8-64b9-532e-a4b6-59198cbb052e" :question/math-academy-id "q-30448"} {:db/id 17592186083187 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082943 :question/id #uuid "f4cf6319-af75-53c4-a5a8-87478b7c3fd0" :question/math-academy-id "e-14836"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e00837a5-acbf-563d-864a-2902fc8e02a9" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083478 :question/id #uuid "eed7af21-0373-53ea-a0ab-29119d366c66" :question/math-academy-id "q-10320"} {:db/id 17592186083621 :question/id #uuid "ae9d95d5-3b55-514f-8c9a-3b7ea84703c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-220360"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Vertex of a Parabola"} {:db/id 17592186082943 :question/id #uuid "f4cf6319-af75-53c4-a5a8-87478b7c3fd0" :question/math-academy-id "e-14836" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186083187 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e00837a5-acbf-563d-864a-2902fc8e02a9" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Vertex of a Parabola"}] :question/problem "Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=-x^2+4x+1$." :question/worked-solution "The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

is given by

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

Substituting $a=-1$ and $b=4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= - (4)/(2(-1)) \\
&= - (4)/((-2)) \\
&= 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=2$. This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we can substitute $x=2$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= -x^{2} + 4x + 1 \\
&= - (2)^{2} + 4(2) + 1 \\
&=-4 + 8 + 1 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(2,5)$."} {:db/id 17592186083478 :question/id #uuid "eed7af21-0373-53ea-a0ab-29119d366c66" :question/math-academy-id "q-10320"} {:db/id 17592186083621 :question/id #uuid "ae9d95d5-3b55-514f-8c9a-3b7ea84703c4" :question/math-academy-id "q-220360"} {:db/id 17592186083188 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082944 :question/id #uuid "dad0da4b-af03-507c-9549-6f5963783da6" :question/math-academy-id "e-14837"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e1ed6e03-7d4f-5606-ab01-3bfdd855348e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050383}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083622 :question/id #uuid "f6cc055d-d8ac-5491-b063-34ee5075a5a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-220361"} {:db/id 17592186083781 :question/id #uuid "a25f9214-8642-59b4-9280-9a388afedbb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-52330"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Unknown Coefficient Given the Axis of Symmetry"} {:db/id 17592186082944 :question/id #uuid "dad0da4b-af03-507c-9549-6f5963783da6" :question/math-academy-id "e-14837" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186083188 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e1ed6e03-7d4f-5606-ab01-3bfdd855348e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Unknown Coefficient Given the Axis of Symmetry"}] :question/problem "The axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=0.25x^2+kx+2$ is $x=-6$. Find the value of $k$." :question/worked-solution "First, we will calculate the axis of symmetry in terms of $k$. Then, we will set our result equal to $-6$.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola

$$
y=ax^2+bx+c
$$

is given by

$$
x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

Substituting $a=0.25$ and $b=k$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= - (k)/(2(0.25)) \\
&=-\frac{k}{0.5} \\
&=-2k
\end{aligned}
$$

We already know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-6$, so we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}
-2k &= -6 \\
k &= 3
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050383} {:db/id 17592186083622 :question/id #uuid "f6cc055d-d8ac-5491-b063-34ee5075a5a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-220361"} {:db/id 17592186083781 :question/id #uuid "a25f9214-8642-59b4-9280-9a388afedbb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-52330"} {:db/id 17592186048812} {:db/id 17592186048939} {:db/id 17592186049712} {:db/id 17592186049828} {:db/id 17592186049982} {:db/id 17592186050577} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186084056} :activity/id #uuid "7b83beeb-cc36-5c10-bc58-518f606a82c6" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048398 :topic/id #uuid "9c16d688-8412-5b64-a180-1b55549f47da" :topic/math-academy-id 704} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186084056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084524 :tutorial/content "To determine the axis of symmetry of the parabola

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}

Suppose we want to find the axis of symmetry of the function

$$
y=3x^2-6x+1
$$

To do this, we substitute $a=3$ and $b=-6$ into the above formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= -\frac{b}{2a} \\
&= - ((-6))/(2(3)) \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=1$ is the equation of the axis of symmetry.

![](images/88/88ee917eb387ee60e67080785519ffe9cb4333adcd602a733659d0447c37f61a.png)

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so $x=1$ also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we can substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= 3x^{2} - 6x + 1 \\
&= 3(1)^{2} - 6(1) + 1 \\
&= 3 - 6 + 1 \\
&=-2
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-2)$.

"aaa6b152-86d3-5f96-8a94-57f86a17a84d" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Flux Over a Surface"}] :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf F(x, y, z) = \left\langle -y, \: x, \: z+2 \right\rangle,
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x^2+y^2$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩{|}_{z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨{{-y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-y,\,x,\,z+2⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot (2x)-(x)\cdot (2y)+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-2xy+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}y+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+2y]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7x}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x-y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨z+y,\,2y+z,\,xy⟩{|}_{z=x-y} \\  & =⟨(x-y)+y,\,2y+(x-y),\,xy⟩ \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{x+y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{xy}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+y,\,2y+z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(x)\cdot 1-(x+y)\cdot (-1)+xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x+x+y+xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(y+xy)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =[2x+{x}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2(1)+{1}^{2})-0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198615 :question/id #uuid "56a2b4c8-31ce-51dd-93f5-6f1083f199f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-161553" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198379 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aaa6b152-86d3-5f96-8a94-57f86a17a84d" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Flux Over a Surface"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "06423401-c4cb-59a0-9bd6-7e1a82b5b0ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3e-2" :db/id 17592186275534} {:answer/id #uuid "0ce5551e-7454-5d22-ae6a-ac13e583b0e7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e-3" :db/id 17592186275587} {:answer/id #uuid "1481a58c-6133-58f7-a21d-cabc8d7625ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2e-2" :db/id 17592186275668} {:answer/id #uuid "7671f819-6d07-506b-b49f-13d0ef633588" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2e-3" :db/id 17592186276546} {:answer/id #uuid "8ab9fbd0-cdfd-51f8-ab82-86979d2a493d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e-2" :db/id 17592186276735}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "1481a58c-6133-58f7-a21d-cabc8d7625ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2e-2" :db/id 17592186275668} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed331e7d-c8f9-522c-8244-24e655efebee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186278141}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Calculate the flux of the vector field

$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨{e}^{x},\,{e}^{y},\,z+1⟩\cdot \text{d}S

$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+y)=2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩{|}_{z=2x+y} \\  & =⟨-x,\,-y,\,xy(2x+y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{{-x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{xy(2x+y)}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x,\,-y,\,xyz⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(-x)\cdot 2-(-y)\cdot (1)+xy(2x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+y+2{x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2xy+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2x+\frac{1}{2}+{x}^{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{7x}{3}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{7{x}^{2}}{6}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{6}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=2\sqrt{xy}$ for $3\le x\le 4$ and $1\le y\le 2.$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\sqrt{xy})=\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\sqrt{xy})=\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the flux of $F$ through $S$ is given by 

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,{z}^{2}+1⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,{z}^{2}+1⟩{|}_{z=2\sqrt{xy}} \\  & =⟨{{\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{4xy+1}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}},\,{z}^{2}+1⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{y}{x}}-\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}+4xy+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-\frac{x}{y}+4xy+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{x}{y}+4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{2}(-\frac{x}{y}+4xy)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}{[-x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+2x{y}^{2}]}_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(-x\operatorname{ln}⁡2+8x+0-2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{4}(6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)x\,\text{d}x \\  & =(6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2){[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\frac{7(6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278548 :question/id #uuid "caf172ee-9d85-5048-a736-0f63395a41ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-161542"} {:db/id 17592186278551 :question/id #uuid "d0720c99-cc1f-5800-96bf-793fcc7002e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-161552"} {:db/id 17592186373972 :question/id #uuid "9a86f1df-9194-5ee6-ac19-2bfbeca02663" :question/math-academy-id "q-161447" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198379 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aaa6b152-86d3-5f96-8a94-57f86a17a84d" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating Flux Over a Surface"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "35f2e086-31b9-544a-9b9a-99a08a27f04e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186373974} {:answer/id #uuid "291af077-cf81-5322-8799-9c4d0a56816f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186373975} {:answer/id #uuid "84fcb1f0-4936-5fbf-afb7-a71a059f4960" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186373976} {:answer/id #uuid "c8544813-339e-5ed8-a745-c0b3a602e975" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186373977} {:answer/id #uuid "c730413b-a101-500a-a942-8a345613f8ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186373978}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "291af077-cf81-5322-8799-9c4d0a56816f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186373975} :answer-field/id #uuid "05d45f19-fa05-53a9-92e1-77a6078e07fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186373973}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the surface integral

$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨y,\,x+z,\,z+2x⟩{|}_{z=y-2x} \\  & =⟨y,\,x+(y-2x),\,y-2x+2x⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y-x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
